NITROGEN ASSESSMENTS IN A CONSTRUCTED AND A NATURAL SALT MARSH OF SAN DIEGO BAY

RENÉ LANGIS, MALGORZATA ZALEJKO, AND JOY B. ZEDLER
Pacific Estuarine Research Laboratory, Department of Biology, San Diego State University, San Diego, California 92182-0057 USA

Abstract. Soil nitrogen pools were lower in a 4-yr-old constructed salt marsh than in an adjacent natural marsh of San Diego Bay. Aboveground biomass and foliar nitrogen content of Spartina foliosa were both lower for the constructed marsh. Soil organic carbon, which was highly positively correlated with total nitrogen, was also lower in the constructed marsh. Rates of nitrogen fixation were higher for the natural marsh in surface soils (1 cm depth) but not in the rhizosphere (10 cm depth). Experimental additions of organic matter increased rates of nitrogen fixation substantially for both the constructed and natural marsh soils, with glucose stimulating greater increases than Spartina foliosa detritus (roots and rhizomes). In comparison with natural marshes studied elsewhere, the San Diego Bay sites have low nitrogen pools and little soil organic carbon. Nitrogen mineralization rates (in situ incubations) were high in both marshes studied. The low nitrogen pools reflect low tidal import and infrequent streamflow influxes and, possibly, high nitrogen demands of vegetation stressed by hypersaline soils.

Key words: mitigation; nitrogen; nitrogen fixation; restoration; salt marsh; soils; Southern California; Spartina foliosa.

INTRODUCTION

Industrial, commercial, residential, and recreational developments along the Southern California coast have destroyed >75% of the region’s coastal wetland area. As habitats have shrunk, several wetland-dependent species have become endangered with extinction. Southern California salt marshes have one endangered plant, and several birds and insects that are considered threatened or endangered with extinction. In San Diego County, only 756 ha of coastal wetland remain; they are distributed among 13 wetlands, which range in size from 0.24 to 171.10 ha (S. Lockhart, personal communication of data from National Wetlands Inventory maps).

Habitat losses continue, as developments and highways expand into wetlands. Mitigation for damages includes attempts to restore degraded wetlands and construct new ones. Because the natural wetlands have been so greatly reduced, it is critical that human-modified habitats replace the ecological functions of natural marshes in order to maintain regional biodiversity (Zedler 1988).

The presence and efficient cycling of nutrients is central to the development and maintenance of marshes, whether they are natural or constructed. Of particular importance in coastal marine environments is nitrogen (Valiela and Teal 1979), which is the primary limiting nutrient in many salt marshes (Howarth 1988), including one in Southern California (Covin and Zedler 1988). Nitrogen levels and availability affect marsh plant productivity, standing biomass, diversity, morphology, reproductive potential, abundance of plant species, and nitrogen content of plant biomass (Valiela 1983). These features in turn influence the invertebrate and vertebrate animals of the wetlands. Inadequate supplies of nitrogen are likely to affect total wetland function, by altering the basic ecosystem processes of primary productivity, decomposition, and food chain support.

Although the role of nitrogen is known to be significant in natural wetlands, there is little information on the nutrient dynamics of constructed salt marshes. Two studies (Lindau and Hossner 1981, Craft et al. 1986, 1988a) are exceptions; both document lower nutrient concentrations in the soils of the constructed wetlands, but the authors reached different conclusions regarding the ability of constructed wetlands to achieve nutrient levels of natural systems.

Lindau and Hossner (1981) compared substrate nutrient levels in constructed and natural marshes on the coast of Texas. Their natural wetlands had low soil organic carbon (<1.3% soil dry mass) and nitrogen content (total N < 600 mg/kg), but levels in the constructed marsh were even lower (<0.5% dry mass and <100 mg/kg, respectively). However, over the 16-mo study period, levels of extractable ammonium and phosphorus, total nitrogen, and organic carbon all increased significantly in the constructed marsh. The increase was attributed to the presence of a dike, which allowed suspended matter and associated nutrients to settle over the dredge spoil substrate. Although all nutrient levels, except phosphorus, remained lower in the constructed marsh than in the natural marsh, the steady

</page>

increases led the authors to believe that the two systems would become comparable in 2–5 yr.

Craft et al. (1986, 1988a) compared total nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic carbon pools in natural and transplanted marsh soils of the North Carolina coast. In most of the natural marshes they studied, the concentrations of organic carbon and nutrients were high (organic C as high as 8.6% and total N up to 1680 mg/kg) compared to the Texas wetlands discussed above. As in Texas, the constructed wetlands in North Carolina had organic matter (≤1.8%) and nutrient levels (total N < 1000 mg/kg) that were lower than in natural marshes. Although the older constructed marshes had higher levels, Craft et al. (1988a) expected constructed marshes to take much longer than 5 yr to match conditions in natural marshes. They predicted that C, N, and P pools associated with macro-organic matter (material retained by a 2-mm mesh sieve) would not approximate levels of the natural marshes for 15–30 yr, and they predicted that the soil nutrient pools would take even longer to develop.

There are few data on the nutrient status of Southern California salt marshes. Studies in Tijuana Estuary suggest that nitrogen levels are low relative to Atlantic and Gulf coast salt marshes. Covin’s (1984) data for inorganic nitrogen suggest low soil nitrogen pools. Winfield (1980) found that the salt marsh filtered inorganic nitrogen from the tidal water, but that the supplies were inadequate for vascular plant and algal needs. He calculated that tidal import could account for only ≈6% of the nitrogen used in marsh primary production. Inflows from the watershed are also limited, since the region’s Mediterranean climate has little rainfall (mean = 25 cm/yr at the coast), which falls during a few storms each year. Although both Winfield (1980) and Covin (1984) indicate that tidal flood waters have high nitrogen content, the runoff moves quickly through the small coastal wetlands. It is thus understandable that the salt marsh vegetation is nitrogen limited, as shown by rapid and significant responses of Spartina foliosa and Salicornia virginica to urea addition (Covin and Zedler 1988).

While nitrogen supplies may be quite limiting for Southern California coastal wetlands, nitrogen demand by the vegetation may be high. The region has high evapotranspiration rates during most of the year; hence, the lower marsh soils are usually hypersaline (35–45 g/kg). Many halophytes are able to allocate nitrogen to the production of nontoxic cytoplasmic osmotica, namely proline and glycinebetaine (Stewart and Lee 1974, Storey and Wyn Jones 1975, Flowers et al. 1977, Wyn Jones et al. 1977). Cavalieri and Huang (1979) observed an increase in proline levels of the salt-marsh grasses, Spartina alterniflora, S. patens, and Distichlis spicata when soil salinity passed a threshold equivalent to that of seawater. Furthermore, Cavalieri (1983) showed that the addition of nitrogen could increase the accumulation of proline and glycinebetaine in S. alterniflora, indicating how strongly the accumulation of these substances is linked to the availability of nitrogen.

If nitrogen demand is high, and inputs from both tidal and stream flows are low, then, either rapid nitrogen recycling or high rates of nitrogen fixation may be necessary to make up the deficit. At Tijuana Estuary, nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria are abundant in the epibenthic algal mats and have high productivity during the warmest months of the year (Zedler 1982). In addition, there is a fair amount of evidence that indicates that free-living bacteria of the rhizosphere can contribute substantially to nitrogen availability (Patriquin et al. 1983). This implies that the contribution of nitrogen fixation in Southern California could be higher than in East Coast salt marshes, where nitrogen fixation was estimated to be only a small component of total nitrogen input (Howarth et al. 1988).

We initiated a study within San Diego Bay to evaluate the nitrogen pools and rates of nitrogen fixation of constructed and natural salt marsh areas dominated by S. foliosa. Studies were restricted to a single intertidal elevation and to adjacent wetlands, in order to reduce hydrologic differences between the comparison sites. We hypothesized that the natural wetland would have greater concentrations of nitrogen and organic carbon and that the vegetation (biomass and foliar nitrogen) would reflect those differences. Nitrogen pools were examined in the sediment (total nitrogen, extractable ammonium, nitrate–nitrite, and organic carbon) and in pore water (ammonium and nitrate–nitrite). Soil samples were incubated in situ to evaluate the capacity of each marsh to transform organic nitrogen into available nitrogen forms. Nitrogen fixation was assessed in the surface soil (to 1 cm) and in the rhizosphere (to 10 cm). Soil organic carbon levels were measured, and experimental amendments (glucose and detritus) helped determined if microbial nitrogen fixers were limited by carbon supplies. Because an earlier study (Swift 1988) had identified significantly lower organic carbon concentrations in the soils of the constructed marsh, we hypothesized that rates of nitrogen fixation would be lower in the subsurface soils, where heterotrophic bacteria might be energy limited.

MATERIALS AND METHODS

Site description

The study site (Fig. 1) is located on the east side of south San Diego Bay within the Sweetwater Marsh National Wildlife Refuge (32°38′ N, 117°6′ W). The refuge is the largest remaining wetland complex in San Diego Bay; it comprises 128 ha, most of which is salt marsh. The constructed salt marsh, known as the Connector Marsh (CM), covers 4.9 ha of formerly disturbed high marsh, salt flats, and upland terrain. In the fall of 1984, the site was graded to create eight lower marsh islands and surrounding creek banks, which were plant-

<page number="3">

ed with S. foliosa from January to March 1985. The constructed site was fertilized on four occasions in 1985–1986 with urea (N addition rate 25 g/m²) (H. Hunt, California Department of Transportation, personal communication). Although fine sediments had accumulated in the channels, the marsh soil was characterized as sandy loam and loamy sand in 1987 (Swift 1988). An air photo from ≈1928 indicates that the entire site was part of the alluvial outwash from Sweetwater River. Dredging and filling along the Bayfront, and use of the wetland as a dump site, raised the topography. Removal of fill was accomplished by the California Department of Transportation as mitigation for widening of Interstate Highway 5, immediately east of the study site.

The selection of a reference site was constrained by hydrologic heterogeneity, which is responsible for both within- and between-marsh soil variability (Mitsch and Gosselink 1986). Because differences in tidal and river inflows are known to determine soil salinity and species composition of the region’s salt marshes (Zedler and Beare 1986), we restricted the choice of a reference wetland to a natural marsh immediately north of the constructed wetland. There were no tidal barriers between the northern portion of the Connector Marsh and Paradise Creek, whereas a tide gate separated the northern part of the Connector Marsh from the southern part, and the Sweetwater River separated the Connector Marsh from other natural wetland remnants. As a further precaution, we selected sampling sites for both marshes at the same intertidal elevation (0.43 m NGVD [Naval Geodetic Vertical Datum]), where S. foliosa was dominant.

The Paradise Creek marsh (PC) covers an area of 10 ha of intertidal salt marsh. The vegetation consists primarily of S. virginica intermixed with S. foliosa, with pure stands of S. foliosa at the elevation selected for sampling. Tidal water moves in through one main meandering tidal creek and a series of secondary creeks. At one time, according to a ≈1928 air photo, the marsh had a separate inlet to San Diego Bay. Later filling and development along the Bayfront blocked that inlet, and a channel was dug straight south, along what is now the eastern margin of the Connector Marsh, so that tide waters entered via the Sweetwater River mouth (Fig. 1).

Nutrient functions were assessed over a 17-mo period, from December 1987 to May 1989, when the constructed marsh was 3–4 yr old. Salinities of low marsh interstitial waters were 27–38 g/kg in the constructed marsh and, 23–36 g/kg in the natural marsh.

Sample collection

The patches of Spartina at the prescribed elevation differed in size; thus long (10–12 m) and short (4 m) transects were used. The short transects were used for nitrogen fixation measurements; these patches were more readily accessible, reducing the delay between field sampling and laboratory incubation. Three short transects were established in each wetland. Samples for all other determinations were collected randomly along the long transects. Four long transects were established in CM and three in PC, where there were fewer areas that met the sampling criteria.

Permanent sampling wells (4–5 per long transect, for a total of 15 at PC and 20 at CM) were installed to collect pore water. Rubber stoppers prevented contamination of pore water by surface water during high tides. Redox potential (using a combination electrode with platinum tip and KCl-filled reference portion) was measured directly in the wells. The electrode was standardized with ZoBell’s solution (0.003 mol/L potassium ferricyanide, 0.003 mol/L potassium ferrocyanide, and 0.1 mol/L potassium chloride) having a Eh of +430 mV at 25°C (ZoBell 1946) and measurements corrected to standard hydrogen electrode values by adding +208 mV to redox readings. A drop of water was also removed to measure salinity with a hand-held temperature-compensated refractometer. Water samples were then collected, put on ice, and taken to the laboratory where they were analyzed for NH₄⁺ within 3 h, frozen, and analyzed for NO₃⁻+NO₂⁻ the same week. Since the volume of water in individual wells depended on the level of the water table at the time of collection, sampling was done as soon as possible after high tide so that a volume of at least 20 mL could be taken. The sampling wells were made out of plastic polyvinyl chloride (PVC) pipes (30 cm long, 2 cm in-

The relatively large mesh size of the screen was needed to favor rapid interstitial water exchange and minimize clogging. Samples were filtered with Whatman GF/C filter paper before analysis. Pore water was sampled quarterly from September 1988 to May 1989.

Aboveground biomass of S. foliosa was determined by clipping all plants in 0.25-m\(^2\) quadrats in July 1989. Three quadrats were randomly selected along each of the long transects. Foliar nitrogen and phosphorus were determined so that N:P ratios could later be estimated as indicators of nitrogen limitation.

Sediment cores (5 cm diameter by 8 cm deep, five per transect) were collected for measurement of total and extractable nitrogen, and organic carbon, using a thin-wall acrylic cylinder. Samples were stored in plastic bags and frozen until they could be analyzed. They were collected in May 1988 and May 1989.

Chemical analyses

Pore water ammonium was determined by the automated phenate method and NO\(_3^-\)+NO\(_2^-\) by the cadmium copper reduction method (APHA 1985). Extractable NH\(_4^+\) and (NO\(_3^-\)+NO\(_2^-\))-N values were obtained by extracting 10 g (wet mass) of a fresh soil sample in 100 mL of 2 mol/L KCl for 1 h and analyzing the extract for NH\(_4^+\) and (NO\(_3^-\)+NO\(_2^-\))-N using the same methods.

Soil water content was estimated by gravimetry and used to calculate all soil chemical contents on a dry mass basis. Bulk density values were used to transform those values to a per volume of soil basis.

Dried samples were analyzed for total Kjeldahl nitrogen (TKN) (APHA 1985) and percent organic carbon by a rapid dichromate oxidation technique (Sims and Haby 1971) after soils were ground with a mortar and pestle and passed through a 2-mm mesh sieve to remove large roots.

Foliar nitrogen and phosphorus were determined on S. foliosa clippings. Plants were washed under deionized water, dried at 60° to constant mass, ground with a Wiley mill, digested by the Kjeldahl method, and the digest analyzed for total nitrogen (APHA 1985) and total phosphorus by the standard molybdate ascorbic acid method (Murphy and Riley 1962).

In situ incubation experiment

We estimated nitrogen mineralization in the field with the buried polyethylene bag technique (Eno 1960). Because plant uptake and leaching of nitrogen is prevented, net mineralization rates can be estimated as the increase in NH\(_4^+\) and NO\(_3^-\)+NO\(_2^-\) (Pastor et al. 1984). Sediment cores (5 cm diameter \(\times\) 8 cm depth) were placed into 0.03 mm thick polyethylene bags; the bags were tied and replaced in their respective holes on 3 May 1988 and covered with \(\approx\) 2 cm of sediment. At the same time another soil core, adjacent to the plastic-enclosed core, was collected and immediately taken to the laboratory for analysis of extractable NH\(_4^+\) and (NO\(_3^-\)+NO\(_2^-\))-N, TKN, and percent organic carbon. A total of 20 bags was installed in CM and 12 in PC along the long transects previously described (see Materials and methods: Sample collection). These polyethylene bags are impermeable to water and permeable to gases such as CO\(_2\) so that constant moisture content can be assured during the incubation while permitting gas exchange (Gordon et al. 1987). On 24 May 1988 the bags were collected and taken back to the laboratory for analysis.

Nitrogen fixation

In addition to the short transects previously described (see Materials and methods: Sample collection), three others were installed across from the northernmost island, on the north bank of CM (Fig. 1). For consistency in comparing marsh areas, results from the north bank are presented separately.

Nitrogen fixation was estimated as nitrogenase activity by the acetylene reduction assay because it is both relatively sensitive and simple to perform (Hardy et al. 1968, Casselman et al. 1981). The other method considered, the \(^{15}\)N assay, is several orders of magnitude less sensitive (Capone 1988) and can require much longer incubation periods to yield meaningful results (Seitzinger and Garber 1987). Nevertheless, the acetylene reduction technique has drawn some criticism, such as the possible effects of contaminating gases associated with acetylene supplies on the metabolism of microorganisms (Hymen and Arp 1987) and the possible stimulating effect of acetylene itself (Topp and Germon 1986). However, since the emphasis of this study was the comparison of two adjacent sites, relative acetylene reduction measures were considered adequate. In addition, because major departures from the stoichiometric 3:1 ratio of moles of C\(_2\)H\(_2\) reduced to moles of N\(_2\) fixed were reported by Seitzinger and Garber (1987) in coastal sediments, nitrogenase activity is expressed as nmoles of C\(_2\)H\(_2\) reduced per surface area.

Samples were collected along short transects randomly selected from dense S. foliosa patches. In the field, two randomly selected sediment cores per transect (10 cm deep by 8 cm in diameter, for root zone nitrogen fixation) were immediately placed upright in 1-L glass mason jars. Each intact core fitted flush against the sides of the jar and had a 300 mL head space. In earlier studies, the highest fixation rates were obtained in the upper 10 cm of soil (Whitney et al. 1975, Hanson 1977, Teal et al. 1979, Casselman et al. 1981) and were attributed to the contribution of photoautotrophs in addition to heterotrophs. Thus, surface cores were also collected. Four small cores (1 cm deep by 3 cm in diameter) were taken within a 20-cm radius of the large cores and carefully placed in 275-mL glass mason jars

with tops facing inward (head space of 245 mL). Air-tight lids (equipped with a serum stopper) were fitted on all jars, which were taken to the laboratory and ac-climated overnight at the incubation temperature of 22° and under a photon flux rate of 10.5 µmol·s⁻¹·m⁻². The 1-L jars were entirely covered with aluminum foil to minimize photoautotrophic C₂H₂ reduction. The next morning, commercial-grade cylinder acetylene (Big 3 Industries, Texas) was added to the jars with a syringe, yielding an atmosphere of 10%. Hyman and Arp (1987) identified several contaminating gases in commercial C₂H₂, mostly hydrogen and hydrocarbon gases; al-though these contaminants could affect absolute C₂H₂ reduction values, their effect on the comparative data of this study could only be minor. The head space gases were mixed by pumping the syringe plunger several times. Gas samples were withdrawn from the jar head space on several occasions after 1.7–5.5 h of incubation. The rates of C₂H₂ reduction were linear over the whole incubation period. Concentrations of C₂H₂ and C₂H₄ were measured with a flame ionization detector on a Varian Vista 6000 gas chromatograph. We in-jected 1-mL samples onto a 2-m Porapak N column (injector temperature: 85°; carrier gas: nitrogen at a 30 mL/min flow rate; oven temperature: 50°). Rates of C₂H₂ reduction were calculated as the difference be-tween means of C₂H₄ concentration measured at two sampling times over that period.

Organic matter amendments

The effect of organic matter additions on the rates of nitrogen fixation was tested using soil samples from three short transects situated in the north bank of CM and in three short transects of PC. The north bank site was chosen because it had low soil organic carbon and was physiographically similar to the PC sites, which were along creek banks. On 2 March 1989, four core samples (1 cm depth, 6.2 cm³) were collected from each of three randomly selected areas within each transect and carefully deposited in 275-mL jars. In the lab-oratory, six jars were amended by equally distributing 2 mL of a freshly prepared glucose solution (10 g/L) to the intact cores with a syringe (final concentration, 2 mg/cm³ of fresh soil), the cores from six other jars were sprinkled with 1 g of detritus and injected with 2 mL H₂O (final concentration, 42 mg/cm³ of fresh soil) and, finally, six other jars (also with four intact cores each) were simply injected with 2 mL H₂O as controls. Glucose was used to evaluate the effect of a readily available energy source. Detritus, which con-sisted of dried and ground S. foliosa roots and rhiz-omes, was used to assess the effect of autochthonous organic matter. Amended and control samples were incubated, and C₂H₂ reduction was performed as pre-viously described (see Materials and methods: Nitrogen fixation).

Statistical analyses

The data distributions were first tested for normality (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test). Within-marsh differences were tested by analysis of variance when distributions were normal and by the nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis test for nonnormal data. If no significant within-marsh differences were detected, data were pooled and a Stu-dent’s t test was applied to the normal data and a Mann-Whitney test to nonnormal data.

Also of importance is the increased subsurface flow of water that is typical on creek banks (Gardner 1973, Agosta 1985). This can be seen within PC by comparing redox potentials of the relatively stagnant waters of one transect with the values obtained at two transects situated along a creek bank (Fig. 3). The lowest redox potentials were measured at the interior site on almost every sampling date except for May and September 1988.

Ammonium levels in the pore water (Table 1) were significantly higher in the natural than in the constructed marsh and an order of magnitude higher on every sampling date except May 1989. The lower value obtained in May could be a result of increased ammonium uptake during rapid plant growth in spring (plants grow at an exponential rate during that period at Tijuana Estuary, according to Winfield 1980). Ammonia measurements in the natural marsh showed high variability (see standard errors, Table 1).

Levels of pore water $NO_3^- + NO_2^-$ were generally low (Table 1), which was to be expected for PC because of the highly reduced condition of its sediments (Fig. 2). Higher $NO_3^- + NO_2^-$ values were expected in the CM samples given the higher redox values of this marsh. The low values obtained are indicative of that marsh's overall lower nitrogen status. Differences in $NO_3^- + NO_2^-$ concentrations between marshes were significant on two of the four sampling sessions (Table 1).

Sediment analyses

Extractable $NH_4^+$ values from PC were significantly higher than in CM for soil samples collected in May 1988 and 1989 (Table 2). This difference was of the same magnitude (3–4-fold) as for the pore water samples collected in May 1989, when the demand for nitrogen by the rapidly growing S. foliosa was high. The 10× difference in pore water values obtained on other sampling periods likely reflects the richer nitrogen content of PC sediments, which is more easily observed during the periods of lower nitrogen demand in summer, fall, and winter. No measurable levels of $NO_3^- + NO_2^-$ were detected in May 1988, which is indicative of active denitrification or nitrate reduction during that period. Differences in extractable $NO_3^- + NO_2^-$ were not significant in May 1989. Extractable $NO_3^- + NO_2^-$ was, as in the case of pore water, much lower than extractable $NH_4^+$.

In situ incubation

Results of the in situ mineralization experiment (Table 4) showed that, although twice as much nitrogen was mineralized in PC as in CM, the relative increases in ammonium in both marshes were similar ($\approx$9$\times$). This indicates that specific mineralization rates were as high in the constructed wetland as in the natural one. Ammonification accounted for almost all of the N mineralization, with net nitrification being much less important. This was to be expected given the low redox conditions of these salt marsh soils (Fig. 2). Levels of nitrates and nitrites were probably kept to low levels, given the high denitrification (Valiela and Teal 1979) and nitrate reduction rates (Nedwell 1982) that are common in salt marsh sediments.

The specific rates of mineralization were too low to cause a significant decrease in percent organic carbon and TKN after 21 d of incubation (Table 4). The increase in ammonium values in both marshes indicates that a significant increase in ammonification can occur without a notable decrease in the organic nitrogen pool, because there were high levels of organic carbon and TKN relative to the inorganic forms of nitrogen.

If we assume specific mineralization rates to remain fairly constant, these results indicate that the supply of inorganic nitrogen to the system could not be limited by the mineralization process per se because specific rates were equivalent. Therefore, the differences in the inorganic nitrogen pools (pore water and extractable nitrogen) should be explained by the difference in labile organic matter pools. In these soils, the labile organic matter fraction likely represents a small portion of total nitrogen or organic matter. Since Spartina density and biomass collected along the same transects (Table 3) were also significantly higher in the natural marsh, plant uptake cannot explain the differences in the inorganic nitrogen content of soils.

These rates account for both heterotrophic and photoautotrophic nitrogen fixation, although the contribution of photoautotrophic nitrogen fixers was probably underestimated because of the low light intensity (10.5 μmol·s⁻¹·m⁻²) under which the samples were incubated. The presence of heterotrophic nitrogen fixers could be inferred by the response of nitrogen-fixing organisms to organic matter amendments (see Results and discussion: Organic matter content and importance). Cyanobacteria, on the other hand, are known to be major nitrogen suppliers among grass stems in salt marshes (Jones 1974, Van Raalte et al. 1974, Carpenter et al. 1978) and were an important part of the productive algal mats found in the nearby Tijuana Estuary (Zedler 1980, 1982).

Results obtained from the 10-cm soil cores, which represented heterotrophic nitrogenase activity in the rhizosphere (they were incubated in the dark), showed a very different pattern. While rates of nitrogen fixation were significantly higher in the natural marsh in December 1987, differences were not significant on the three following assay dates, and rates were significantly higher in the constructed marsh (including north bank) in September 1988.

The different pattern observed between the surface and rhizosphere assays is indicative of the complex interaction of the multiple factors affecting nitrogen fixation in coastal sediments. In the surface cores, we can speculate that higher levels of organic matter in PC stimulate rates of nitrogen fixation. In the deep cores this effect of organic matter was possibly masked by the relatively high levels of soil ammonium in the natural marsh. Ammonium has been shown to inhibit nitrogen fixation in salt marsh sediments and in microflora associated with the rhizosphere (Teal et al. 1979, Casselman et al. 1981, Yoch and Whiting 1986). The high pore water (Table 1) and extractable ammonium values found in PC (Table 2) support this explanation. Casselman et al. (1981) showed that nitrogen fixation was inversely related to extractable ammonium levels; zero rates were measured at NH₄⁺ levels higher than 20 μg/g. In the case of surface cores, ammonium concentrations could be lower than the threshold for the switch-off of nitrogenase activity, be-

Seasonal effects could explain the low rates of nitrogen fixation obtained in the December 1987 deeper cores and to a certain extent in the February 1988 surface cores. Since the assay jars were incubated overnight at 22\( ^\circ \)C, only the effect of temperature on the physiological status of the microbial population at the time of sampling could explain lower rates of nitrogen fixation for the surface and deeper cores. The stimulatory effect of plant roots on nitrogenase activity is well established (Casselman et al. 1981).

Organic matter content and importance

Soil organic carbon was consistently higher in the natural marsh (Table 2). In addition, percent organic carbon was highly correlated with total sediment nitrogen (\( r = 0.95 \), Fig. 4), which indicates that organic matter is an important potential source of available nitrogen. We also found a significant correlation with rates of nitrogen fixation (\( r = 0.74 \)); this was expected, given that organic carbon is an essential energy source for nitrogen fixation.

Addition of organic matter in the form of Spartina detritus (roots and rhizomes) had a significant effect on the rates of nitrogen fixation (Fig. 5), showing the importance and potential contribution of organic matter produced belowground. Craft et al. (1988b) used stable carbon isotopes to show that emergent vegetation was the major contributor to marsh soil organic carbon in natural and transplanted estuarine marshes of North Carolina. Since only a small part of the aboveground vegetation was shown to be added to marsh organic carbon, the contribution of rhizomes and roots, which are most dense between 5 and 10 cm depth, is considered to be most important (Oenema and De-Laune 1988). More substantial stimulation of rates of nitrogen fixation was obtained in both marshes when glucose was added to the cores (Fig. 5). This implies that the more refractory detrital organic compounds cannot be utilized by the nitrogen fixers and must be decomposed into simpler compounds. While the assay also showed that both marshes were equally limited in organic matter, the positive response of the constructed marsh indicates how nitrogen cycling might be manipulated by adding organic matter.

Ecological applications

As for the Texas (Lindau and Hossner 1981) and North Carolina studies (Craft et al. 1986, 1988a), the San Diego Bay constructed marsh had lower levels of nutrients and organic carbon than the adjacent natural marsh (Table 6). Although organic carbon and nitrogen levels for natural marshes from the three areas are comparable (Table 6), they are somewhat low when compared with nutrient levels of marshes from Massachusetts, Rhode Island, or Louisiana (Valiela 1983).

Four years after construction and planting with Spartina, the constructed marsh has not developed nutrient pools that are comparable to those of an adjacent natural marsh. The 12-mo study period was not long enough to see significant increases in pore water and extractable ammonium, or in total sediment nitrogen
</page>

<page number="10">

and percent organic carbon. The response of nitrogen fixation to organic matter amendments indicated that the process is energy limited. The mineralization experiment showed that specific microbial activity was similar but that total mineralization was twice as high in the natural marsh. Therefore, low nutrient levels in the constructed marsh result from the poorer organic matter pool of the constructed marsh. Several years will be necessary for soil organic matter in the constructed marsh to reach levels permitting a steady-state supply of mineralized nutrients. In Southern California, where year-round mild temperatures are favorable to high mineralization rates, the accumulation of organic matter will be even slower. In addition, a mineralization model for marsh sediments developed by Morris and Bowden (1986) demonstrated that mature marshes with deep sediments are more efficient at recycling nitrogen and phosphorus than young marshes with shallow sediments.

At some mitigation sites, the soils of constructed marshes have been fertilized with urea to accelerate plant growth. However, pulsed nitrogen additions can have undesirable impacts, such as increased insect herbivory and defoliation, which could set back ecosystem development. Such an event occurred at another San Diego Bay mitigation site, where herbivorous scale insects accompanied the S. foliosa transplants, but the natural control agent (a carnivorous beetle) did not (K. Williams, San Diego State University, personal communication). Incorporation of organic matter before planting should have greater potential, as nitrogen would be supplied gradually with decomposition, and nitrogen fixation processes would develop to sustain supplies.

The question of whether or not constructed wetlands will ever duplicate the nutrient cycling function of natural salt marshes remains. Although we have examined the nitrogen pools of only one constructed marsh, and have limited information on the region's natural marsh remnants, our results suggest that mitigation be undertaken cautiously. Exchanging an acre of constructed wetland for an acre of natural wetland results in a net loss in wetland function. Based on the data for Tijuana Estuary (Winfield 1980, Covin 1984, Covin and Zedler 1988) and Paradise Creek Marsh, we believe that nitrogen supplies and availability are close to critical limits. The likelihood that constructed wetlands will have even lower pools of nitrogen and organic matter means that the nutritional status and productivity of the vegetation in human-made salt marshes will be even more severely limited. These predictions are borne out by the lower biomass and foliar nitrogen concentrations of S. foliosa in CM, compared to PC. Presumably, these differences in the vegetation also affect invertebrate and vertebrate consumers of the CM. A study of epibenthic invertebrates (Rutherford 1989) has documented substantially lower abundances in CM than in PC. Since we do not yet know how long it will take for low-nutrient, inorganic soils to build up sufficient organic matter and nitrogen pools that match those of natural wetlands, the time required for constructed marshes to become functionally equivalent to natural salt marshes cannot be predicted.

If nitrogen fixation, tidal inflows, groundwater, and streamflows are not major components of the nitrogen budget of these Southern California marshes, what is the nitrogen source? The mineralization data suggest that the ecosystem relies on nitrogen recycling. If this is true, then the ecosystem is relying on nitrogen pools that build up very slowly.

Results obtained from the 10-cm soil cores, which represented heterotrophic nitrogenase activity in the rhizosphere (they were incubated in the dark), showed a very different pattern. While rates of nitrogen fixation were significantly higher in the natural marsh in December 1987, differences were not significant on the three following assay dates, and rates were significantly higher in the constructed marsh (including north bank) in September 1988. The different pattern observed between the surface and rhizosphere assays is indicative of the complex interaction of the multiple factors affecting nitrogen fixation in coastal sediments. In the surface cores, we can speculate that higher levels of organic matter in PC stimulate rates of nitrogen fixation. Nitrogen sources and net growth efficiency of zooplankton in three Amazon River plume food webs Natalie Loick-Wilde,a,*1 Sarah C. Weber,1 Brandon J. Conroy,2 Douglas G. Capone,3 Victoria J. Coles,4 Patricia M. Medeiros,5 Deborah K. Steinberg,2 Joseph P. Montoya1 1School of Biology at Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 2Virginia Institute of Marine Science, College of William & Mary, Gloucester Point, Virginia 3University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 4University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science, Horn Point Laboratory, Cambridge, Maryland 5Department of Marine Sciences, University of Georgia, Athens, Georgia Abstract The plasticity of nitrogen specific net growth efficiency (NGE) in marine mesozooplankton is currently unresolved, with discordant lines of evidence suggesting that NGE is constant, or that it varies with nitrogen source, food availability, and food quality in marine ecosystems. Specifically, the fate of nitrogen from nitrogen fixation is poorly known. We use \(^{15}\mathrm{N} : \ ^{14}\mathrm{N}\) ratios in plankton in combination with hydrological data, nutrient profiles, and nitrogen fixation rate measurements to investigate the relationship between new nitrogen sources and the nitrogen specific NGE in three plankton communities along the outer Amazon River plume. The NGE of small (200–500 \( \mu \mathrm{m} \)) mesozooplankton was estimated from the \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) differences between particulate nitrogen and zooplankton using an open system Rayleigh fractionation model. The transfer efficiency of nitrogen among larger (> 500 \( \mu \mathrm{m} \)) mesozooplankton was estimated from the change in \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) as a function of zooplankton size. The Amazon River was not a significant source of bioavailable nitrogen anywhere in our study region, and subsurface nitrate was the primary new nitrogen source for the outer shelf community, which was dominated by diatoms. N\(_2\) fixation was the principal new nitrogen source at sites of high diatom diazotroph association abundance and at oceanic sites dominated by *Trichodesmium* spp. and *Synechococcus* spp. Although we found clear spatial differences in food quantity, food quality, and diazotroph inputs into mesozooplankton, our data show no significant differences in mesozooplankton nitrogen transfer efficiency and NGE (for latter, mean ± SD: 59 ± 10%) among sites. The movement of new nitrogen through pelagic food webs is critical to marine secondary production and the efficiency of nitrogen transfer may be especially sensitive to changes in phytoplankton community structure associated with climate change (Hutchins et al. 2007; Paerl and Huisman 2008). In zooplankton, the proportion of assimilated nitrogen that is used for growth is called the nitrogen net growth efficiency (NGE), a critical, but poorly constrained parameter in biogeochemical models (Touratier et al. 2001; Anderson et al. 2013; Mitra et al. 2014). A variety of controlled laboratory experiments (Checkley 1980; Berggreen et al. 1988; Kiorboe 1989) suggest that zooplankton NGE is consistently around 45% (Touratier et al. 1999; Touratier et al. 2001), while field studies suggest that NGE is much more variable, ranging from 18% to 72% (Le Borgne 1982 and references therein), and sensitive to food quality as shown by the model of Anderson and Hessen (1995). The movement of nitrogen (N) through the phytoplankton into the mesozooplankton community can be tracked and quantified by means of stable nitrogen isotope analysis (Peterson and Fry 1987). The natural abundance of stable nitrogen isotopes in plankton reflects the sources of N supporting biological production, as well as the physiological processes that may alter isotopic abundance within the ecosystem (Montoya et al. 2002; Martínez Del Rio et al. 2009). The \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) (\( \%_o \) deviation in \(^{15}\mathrm{N} : \ ^{14}\mathrm{N}\) between a sample and atmospheric N\(_2\)) of mesozooplankton and particulate organic nitrogen (PN) in particular reflect the origin, movement, and transformation of nitrogen in the upper water column (Goering et al. 1990; Fry and Quiñones 1994; Benner et al. 1997). The NGE of mesozooplankton can be estimated from the difference in the \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of mesozooplankton and PN (\( \Delta \delta \)) if the physiological processes that fractionate the nitrogen isotopes are accounted for (Montoya 2007; Montoya 2008). The release of \( ^{15}\mathrm{N}\)-depleted ammonium (\( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \)) through excretion appears to play a pivotal role in enriching an animal’s tissues in \( ^{15}\mathrm{N} \), typically by 2%–4% relative to its diet (Minagawa and Wada 1984; Bada et al. 1989; Gannes et al. 1997). The major factors that can affect \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) excretion rates of ammonotelic (ammonium excreting) zooplankton include temperature, body size, nutritional status, food quality, light, and salinity, whereas the principal feeding mode (e.g., carnivory, herbivory, or detritivory) does not appear to have a strong effect on excretion rate (reviewed by Steinberg and Saba 2008). From a physiological point of view, the increase in \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) with trophic position (trophic effect) results from the partitioning of assimilated dietary nitrogen between new biomass and \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) excretion (Montoya 2008). In other words, the greater the fraction of assimilated nitrogen released through excretion, the greater the trophic effect and the higher the resulting \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of the animal’s biomass. PN and mesozooplankton differ in their turnover times and in the type of information they provide on ecological processes over time scales of hours to weeks (Montoya 2007). The \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of PN is sensitive to the sources of N (e.g., nitrate, ammonium, \( \mathrm{N}_2 \)) and the uptake mechanisms supporting production (Minagawa and Wada 1986; Carpenter et al. 1997; Waser et al. 2000). This baseline \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) can be modified by transient events including phytoplankton blooms driven by the injection of subthermocline nitrate into surface waters or by inputs of regenerated ammonium from heterotrophs (Altabet 1989; Waser et al. 2000). Repeated sampling of PN in the water column and vertical integration of the \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of PN can provide a measure of the average isotopic state of the upper water column (Altabet and McCarthy 1985; Montoya et al. 2002; Montoya 2007). The \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of zooplankton integrates over longer time scales that reflect animal growth rates, and is, therefore, less sensitive to transient events than the \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of PN (Montoya 2007). The difference in \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) between PN and zooplankton at any time is thus a time-averaged value that reflects the cumulative impact of the animal’s feeding and excretory processes over the animal’s characteristic N turnover time. This in turn provides an estimate of the “time integrated” NGE in the planktonic food web (Montoya 2007). A number of lines of isotopic evidence indicate that the incorporation of nitrogen from diazotrophic (\( \mathrm{N}_2 \)-fixing) phytoplankton into mesozooplankton at oligotrophic sites is highly efficient, and may be more efficient than zooplankton incorporation of nitrogen from phytoplankton supported by nitrate in more eutrophic waters. For the tropical North Atlantic, relevant observations include high in situ incorporation rates of diazotroph nitrogen into mesozooplankton (O’Neil et al. 1995), small differences in \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) among zooplankton size fractions (Montoya et al. 2002), and correlations between \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) values of amino acids from *Trichodesmium* and various zooplankton size fractions (McClelland et al. 2003). Furthermore, high in situ diazotroph nitrogen incorporation rates into the amino acid nitrogen of mesozooplankton have been observed in the Baltic Sea (Loick-Wilde et al. 2012). Diverse \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixing communities occur in tropical river-ocean systems like the Amazon or Mekong River plumes, where multiple allochthonous and autochthonous nitrogen sources may be important (Voss et al. 2006; Foster et al. 2007; Moisander et al. 2008). In such dynamic systems, a variety of hydrographic (e.g., T, S, nutrient concentrations), biological (e.g., community composition and rates of activity), and biogeochemical (e.g., \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) and \( \delta^{13}\mathrm{C} \)) measurements provide insight into the dominant organic and inorganic N sources supporting different plankton communities (Fry and Sherr 1984; Voss et al. 2006; Loick et al. 2007). Here, we present a comprehensive set of isotopic measurements of dissolved organic carbon, particulate organic carbon, particulate organic nitrogen, and mesozooplankton collected in the outer Amazon River plume in the context of hydrological, chemical, and biological measurements from the same cruise. A recent paper by Goes et al. (2014) described the phytoplankton biogeography of the Amazon plume system based on data collected during the same cruise, identifying three distinct communities, two of which are driven by \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixation, either by “diatom-diazotroph” associations (DDAs), or by colonial cyanobacteria belonging to the genus *Trichodesmium* and unicellular *Synechococcus* spp. The third major phytoplankton community of Goes et al. (2014) is dominated by diatoms that lack diazotrophic symbionts. We test the hypothesis that the NGE of epipelagic mesozooplankton is highest at sites where \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) is the principal new nitrogen source supporting primary production. We first identify and quantify the new nitrogen sources for the upper water column, then estimate and compare mesozooplankton NGE at three sites representative of the three distinct phytoplankton assemblages. *Materials and methods* Samples were collected during the R/V *Knorr* cruise KN197 (22 May 2010–22 June 2010) to the western tropical North Atlantic and outer Amazon River plume (Fig. 1; http://www.rvdata.us/catalog/KN197-08). A Seabird SBE-911 plus CTD-rosette system was used to measure hydrographic properties and collect water samples through the upper water column. Samples for inorganic nutrients (SiO\(_2\), NO\(_3\) + NO\(_2\), and PO\(_4\)) were collected unfiltered from the rosette and analyzed at Fig. 1. Station map along the Amazon River Plume salinity gradient sampled in May 2010–June 2010. Stations selected are focused on those for which the dominant phytoplankton communities according to Goes et al. (2014) were identified as given in the color code. Station 6 and stations close to the shelf for which additional nutrient data was available (12 and 13) are also shown. Zooplankton isotopes were sampled during multiple tows at 10 stations (underlined). sea using a Lachat QuikChem 8000 flow-injection analyzer, with an analytical precision for nitrate plus nitrite of ±0.2 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\). NH\(_4^+\) concentration was measured at sea fluorometrically according to Taylor et al. (2007), with a precision of ± 0.02 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\). Suspended particles were collected by gentle pressure filtration of 2–17 L of seawater through pre-combusted (450\(^\circ\)C for 2 h) 47-mm GF/F filters that were dried at 60\(^\circ\)C and stored over desiccant for analysis ashore. For isotopic analysis, filters containing particle samples were trimmed, and cut into quadrants or halves that were pelletized in tin capsules. Filters with uneven distribution of material were first ground to homogenize the sample, weighed, and subsampled for analysis. Zooplankton were collected in oblique tows using a 1-m\(^2\) Multiple Opening-Closing Net and Environmental Sensing System (MOCNESS; 202- \( \mu \)m mesh size) through the upper water column during the day and at night. Typically, the MOCNESS sampling depth intervals in the upper 100 m were: 0–25 m, 25–50 m, 50–100 m or 0–25 m, 25–50 m, 50–75 m, and 75–100 m. Zooplankton samples from each net were split with either a quarter or half of the sample preserved immediately in 4% buffered formaldehyde for taxonomic analysis. The remainder of the samples were size-fractionated using nested sieves with mesh sizes of 5000 \( \mu \)m, 2000 \( \mu \)m, 1000 \( \mu \)m, 500 \( \mu \)m, and 200 \( \mu \)m and then transferred onto preweighed disks of 200 \( \mu \)m Nitex mesh (Steinberg et al. 2012) for biomass and gut pigment measurements, and nitrogen and carbon elemental and isotopic analyses. All plankton size fractions were visually inspected for major taxa present using a stereo microscope (6–60X magnification) before being frozen (–20\(^\circ\)C) at sea. Ashore, these samples were subsequently thawed and dried at 60\(^\circ\)C for 24 h and weighed to determine biomass. The samples were then ground to a fine powder and subsampled for nitrogen and carbon elemental and isotopic analysis. All natural abundance measurements of particulate and zooplankton nitrogen and carbon were made by continuous-flow isotope-ratio mass spectrometry (CF-IRMS) using a Micromass Optima interfaced to a CE NC2500 elemental analyzer. Particulate organic carbon (PC) samples for \( \delta^{13} \)C analysis generally were not acidified, as calcifying organisms were not a significant component of the phytoplankton communities (E. J. Carpenter unpubl. data). All isotope abundances are expressed as \( \delta^{15} \)N values relative to atmospheric N\(_2\) and as \( \delta^{13} \)C values relative to VPDB. Each analytical run included a size series of elemental (methionine) and isotopic (peptone) standards, which provided a check on stability of the instrument and allowed us to remove the contribution of any analytical blank from our isotopic measurements (Montoya 2008). In general our analytical blank was < 0.3 \( \mu \)mol C and < 0.15 \( \mu \)mol N. We conservatively estimate that the overall analytical precisions of our concentration and isotopic measurements are better than ± 0.15 \( \mu \)mol for nitrogen, ± 0.3 \( \mu \)mol for carbon, and ±0.15\(^\circ\) for both \( \delta^{15} \)N and \( \delta^{13} \)C. We estimated mixed layer depths from the maximum in the buoyancy frequency of the water column (Turner 1980). The depth of the nitracline was taken as the shallowest depth where nitrate plus nitrite was found, and was compared to the vertical \( \delta^{15} \)N PN structure associated with the nitrate uptake of phytoplankton (Montoya et al. 1992; Altabet 1996) to identify changes in the nitracline depth associated with the lateral advection of shelf waters along the flow of the river plume. N\(_2\) fixation rates were measured according to Montoya et al. (1996) using \(^{15}\)N\(_2\) gas from Cambridge (98% \(^{15}\)N\(_2\)) with triplicate incubations in 4.6 L Nalgene bottles typically using water from six depths in the upper 100 m of the water Loick-Wilde et al. We note that our estimates of N$_2$ fixation may be conservative due to the time required for equilibration of $^{15}N_2$ gas with the incubation medium (Mohr et al. 2010; Dabundo et al. 2014). Dabundo et al. (2014) also caution that $^{15}N$-ammonium contamination in $^{15}N_2$ gas from Cambridge may lead to an overestimation of N$_2$ fixation rates by 0.0008 nmol L$^{-1}$ h$^{-1}$, but we had multiple experiments where $^{15}N$ incorporation into biomass was undetectable, especially at ES stations indicating minimal to nonexistent contamination by $^{15}N$-ammonium or other bioavailable N species. Our experimental bottles were incubated under simulated in situ conditions for 24 h, then terminated by gentle pressure filtration (10–15 psi) onto precombusted GF/F filters after passage through a 10 $\mu$m prefilter. This filtration scheme produced large (> 10 $\mu$m) and small (< 10 $\mu$m) size fractions to separate N$_2$ fixation by unicellular and larger diazotrophs like DDAs or Trichodesmium (Agawin et al. 2014 and references therein). Areal N$_2$ fixation rates were calculated by trapezoidal integration from the surface to 100 m depth or to the seafloor, whichever was shallower. Contributions of DOM Samples collected during our cruise for measurement of DON concentrations were damaged during transport (P. L. Yager pers. comm.). We, therefore, use measurements of the concentration and $\delta^{13}C$ of DOC from the same cruise (Medeiros et al. 2015) to estimate the potential contribution of dissolved organic nitrogen to particles in our investigation area. Specifically, we used the relationship between sea surface salinity and the concentration and $\delta^{13}C$ of DOC to define the conservative mixing line for $\delta^{13}C$ DOC after Cai et al. (1988) using the endmember values in Table 1, then applied a literature value for the C: N ratio of Amazon DOM (Hedges et al. 1994) to estimate the potential nitrogen inputs to our study area via transport of DOM. Quantification of diazotroph N in PN and zooplankton We used the "concentration weighted" and depth-integrated $\delta^{15}N$ of PN (in the following termed $\delta^{15}N_{NCD}$) as a proxy for the isotopic composition of the base of the pelagic food web. We carried out a trapezoidal integration from the surface to the depth of the nitracline (Montoya et al. 1992) as follows: Weighted Mean $\delta^{15}N_{NCD} = \frac{\sum ([PN]_i \times \Delta z_i \times \delta^{15}N_i)}{\sum ([PN]_i \times \Delta z_i)}$ (1) where [PN]$_i$ represents the particulate nitrogen concentration ($\mu$mol L$^{-1}$), $\delta^{15}N_i$ represents the isotopic composition of suspended particles, and $\Delta z_i$ is the depth interval (m) represented by sample i. The individual layers, of thickness $\Delta z$, were bounded by the midpoints between sample depths, and the integration extended from the surface to the nutricline depth. At stations that showed changes in water masses during extended PN and zooplankton sampling (Stas. 2, 6, 19, 20, 23, 25, and 27, see Supporting Information Fig. S1 for water mass analysis), we used the PN profile from the CTD cast that was nearest in time to the MOCNESS tow for comparison to zooplankton. We used zooplankton from the 0–25 m and the 25–50 m depth strata to estimate the contribution of diazotroph N to the planktonic food web. This approach should minimize the potential impact of isotopically enriched particles from below the nitracline, providing a robust estimate of the inputs of diazotroph N in the surface mixed layer (Altabet 1989; Landrum et al. 2011). The diazotroph N contribution was calculated for both particles and mesozooplankton using the isotope mass balance approach of Montoya et al. (2002). The contribution of diazotroph nitrogen to suspended particles was calculated as: % Diazotroph N = $100 \times \left( \frac{\delta^{15}N_{NCD} - \delta^{15}N_{Nitrate}}{\delta^{15}N_{Diazo} - \delta^{15}N_{Nitrate}} \right)$ (2) where $\delta^{15}N_{NCD}$ is the weighted mean $\delta^{15}N_{PN}$ of PN calculated using Eq. 1, $\delta^{15}N_{Nitrate}$ is the isotopic endmember of 4.5‰ for deep-water nitrate (Knapp et al. 2008), and $\delta^{15}N_{Diazo}$ is the isotopic endmember of -2‰ for N$_2$ fixation into particles (Montoya et al. 2002). The contribution of diazotroph nitrogen to mesozooplankton biomass was calculated as: % Diazotroph N = $100 \times \left( \frac{\delta^{15}N_{Zoo} - \delta^{15}N_{Reference\ Zoo}}{\delta^{15}N_{Diazo} - \delta^{15}N_{Reference\ Zoo}} \right)$ (3) where $\delta^{15}N_{Zoo}$ is the $\delta^{15}N$ value of one of the five zooplankton size fractions collected from each depth interval sampled, $\delta^{15}N_{Diazo}$ is the isotopic endmember of -2‰ for diazotrophic N, and $\delta^{15}N_{Reference\ Zoo}$ is a reference $\delta^{15}N$ for zooplankton collected in regions not heavily influenced by 463 consumption of diazotroph nitrogen as described by Landrum et al. (2011). These reference values provide an index to the scaling of \( \delta^{15}N \) with animal size, and the low reference values we used provide a conservative estimate of the diazotroph contribution to biomass. Estimation of the nitrogen specific net growth efficiency We used an open system Rayleigh fractionation model for the steady state case where the amount of N incorporated through feeding is equal to the amount of N lost through excretion as described by Montoya (2007). We are focusing on the steady state by minimizing the impact of the natural temporal variability in \( \delta^{15}N \) by eliminating all stations with evidence for recent changes in \( \delta^{15}N \) and estimated NGE only for stations where the observed variability of the \( \delta^{15}N \) PN values above the nitracline and the zooplankton \( \delta^{15}N \) values from the 0–25 m and the 25–50 m depth strata was < 1‰. At steady state, we then look at the partitioning of isotopes required to produce the enrichment in \( ^{15}N \) we observe in the zooplankton size fractions under the assumption that excretion is the only process that significantly affects the \( \Delta\delta^{15}N \) that we measured: \[ \delta^{15}N_{Zoo} = \delta^{15}N_{NCD} - \varepsilon \times \ln f \] where \( \delta^{15}N_{Zoo} \) is the \( \delta^{15}N \) value of the smallest zooplankton size fraction (200–500 \( \mu \)m) in a specific depth stratum (50–25 m or 25–0 m), \( \varepsilon \) is the isotopic enrichment factor of −2.7‰ for NH\(_4^+\) excretion by zooplankton (Checkley and Miller 1989), and \( \delta^{15}N_{NCD} \) is the weighted mean \( \delta^{15}N \) of PN between the surface and the nitracline (Eq. 1). Equation 4 can be rearranged to yield an expression for \( f \), the fraction of assimilated nitrogen remaining in the animal’s body: \[ f = \exp \left( \frac{\delta^{15}N_{NCD} - \delta^{15}N_{Zoo}}{\varepsilon} \right) \] which is equivalent to the NGE of the animal. Using a value of \( \varepsilon = -2.7\% \) and an isotopic difference (\( \Delta\delta^{15}N = \delta^{15}N_{NCD} - \delta^{15}N_{Zoo} \)) of 3‰, for example, implies a NGE of 0.33% or 33%. Note that the substrate pool for deamination and excretion in an actively feeding animal would be weighted toward the food consumed. Under these conditions, an animal will release NH\(_4^+\) with a \( \delta^{15}N \) lower than that of the food consumed and more than 2.7‰ lower than the \( \delta^{15}N \) of the animal’s tissues (Frazer et al. 1997). Therefore, this simple approach provides an upper limit for the overall efficiency of transfer of nitrogen through the food web to a particular size fraction of zooplankton (Montoya 2007). For more complex situations with time-varying diet, we refer to the Ramesh-Singh model (Ramesh and Singh 2010). For larger zooplankton (size fractions > 500 \( \mu \)m), we used the slopes of the linear regressions of \( \delta^{15}N_{Zoo} \) as a function of size as an index to N transfer efficiency among the different zooplankton size fractions from the upper 50 m as in Montoya et al. (2002). Results Goes et al. (2014) identified three distinct phytoplankton communities separated largely on the basis of salinity gradients across the plume (Fig. 1). These three assemblages included an Estuarine Type (ES) Community located upstream of the plume on the shelf at salinities below 28 and comprised of a high biomass mixed population of diatoms, dinoflagellates, cryptophytes, and green-water *Synechococcus* spp. A second, coastal Mesohaline (MH) Community was located in the northwestern region of the plume off the shelf at salinities between 28 and 35 and contained abundant Diatom-Diazotroph Associations (DDAs, mostly *Hemiaulus* sp./*Richelia* sp.). The third, Oceanic (OC) Community was dominated by *Trichodesmium* spp. and oceanic *Synechococcus* spp. in the oligotrophic offshore waters outside of the plume with salinities above 35. DDAs, *Trichodesmium* spp., and *Synechococcus* spp. are all capable of N\(_2\) fixation (Mitsui et al. 1986; Carpenter and Capone 2008), while the dominant phytoplankton in the Estuarine Type Community must rely on other N sources for growth. We additionally separated the MH community into two subgroups, MH1 and MH2. These two MH groups differed in multiple ways, including their nutrient concentrations (MH1 > MH2, Table 2), DDA cell abundance at the surface (MH1 \( \ll \) MH2), and the relatively low abundances or absence of asymbiotic diatoms at MH2 stations (Goes et al. 2014). Station 23 was unique in that it was the only station with moderate DDA abundances and high N\(_2\) fixation rates despite having low salinity comparable to shelf waters at ES stations, and, therefore, is listed separately in Table 2. Station 21 had a sea surface salinity below 35 (33.6) but was dominated by *Trichodesmium* spp. and oceanic *Synechococcus* spp. according to Goes et al. (2014), and therefore was also listed separately in Table 2. Station 6 was not included in the study of Goes et al. (2014) but was characteristic of an OC station (Table 2), including dominance by *Trichodesmium* spp. (R. A. Foster unpubl. data) and, therefore, classified as an OC station. Stations 12 and 13 were not classified by Goes et al. (2014) but nutrient data for these two shelf stations were added for a higher resolution of nutrient distribution at ES stations (Figs. 3, 4). Discussion The relatively few studies to date that have explored the NGE of zooplankton indicate a clear divergence between nearly constant NGE values measured in controlled laboratory experiments (summarized by Touratier et al. 1999) and variable NGE estimates from field measurements (Le Borgne 1982 and references therein). This discrepancy contributes to large uncertainties regarding the role of zooplankton in biogeochemical cycles (Anderson et al. 2013). Our stable nitrogen isotope approach (Montoya 2007) provides a robust, “time integrated” estimate of the NGEs of mesozooplankton (200–500 \( \mu \mathrm{m} \)) from the outer Amazon River plume and adjacent oceanic waters. Interestingly, our data showed no correlation between mesozooplankton NGE and the contribution of diazotroph nitrogen to particles, food quality as reflected in PN: PC ratios, or food quantity as measured by PN and Chl \( a \) concentrations (not shown). Our findings thus corroborate earlier suggestions from laboratory experiments and modeling exercises that mesozooplankton may adjust their feeding behavior in response to changes in food quality and quantity in order to maintain constant nitrogen specific net growth efficiencies and elemental (C: N) ratios in their tissues. Besides the river plume, the onshore advection of nutrient rich North Brazilian Current water (Demaster and Pope 1996), and anticyclonic (warm core) and cyclonic (cold core) North Brazilian Current rings (Fratantoni and Richardson 2006) may have a marked impact on the hydrology and biological activity of the shelf and in offshore waters between the equator and 10°N. Previous studies of the nutrient systematics in the Amazon River and its plume have shown nitrogen to be the most limiting nutrient for algal growth in both shelf (Demaster and Pope 1996) and offshore waters (Cooley and Yager 2006; Cooley et al. 2007). The Amazon River carries high concentrations of silicate (14–150 µmol L⁻¹) and phosphate (0.6–0.8 µmol L⁻¹) but nitrate concentrations of 12–23 µmol L⁻¹ are low compared to other large rivers like the Pearl (Cai et al. 2004) or Mississippi Rivers (Dagg et al. 2004), where nitrate concentrations are typically higher than 75 µmol L⁻¹. Within the plume, this nutrient composition leads to strong N limitation of algal growth at the outer Amazon shelf (4–5°N) where silicate and phosphate concentrations remain high (Demaster and Pope 1996). Algal blooms are nevertheless present on the outer Amazon shelf during all seasons (summarized by Demaster and Pope 1996). The depletion of dissolved inorganic nitrogen we observed in the river plume (Fig. 3A) and the shoaling of the nitracline into surface waters at the ES stations (Fig. 4A) are both consistent with an important role for advective inputs of nitrate-rich subplume waters in supporting primary production on the shelf.
