fixation rates for all streams, those with lower uptake rates tended to have higher fixation rates (r = 0.685, \( p = 0.133 \)). For the pristine prairie stream Kings K2A, the rate of N\(_2\) fixation is about 15% of the NO\(_3^-\) uptake rate (on an areal basis). This suggests that N\(_2\) fixation can be a significant contributor to stream N budgets. However, for our other pristine prairie stream Kings N4D, the N\(_2\)-fixation rate was only 2% of the NO\(_3^-\) uptake rate. None of the other streams had N\(_2\)-fixation rates that were more than 6% of their NO\(_3^-\) uptake rates, with the Big Blue Ditch value being only 0.02%. Taken together, this suggests that the impact of N\(_2\) fixation to the N budget of small streams is variable. While N\(_2\) fixation may be a substantial contributor in streams with low chronic N loads, this does not appear to be consistent, and N\(_2\) fixation does not seem to be a substantial contributor to N budgets in small streams with higher chronic N loads. This is in agreement with previous studies, both in terms of the variability observed across streams, but also in concluding that N\(_2\) fixation can be important in certain oligotrophic streams and perhaps only at certain times (Marcarelli and Wurtsbaugh 2007; Marcarelli et al. 2008; Scott et al. 2009; Lang et al. 2012; Kunza and Hall 2013, 2014).

Patchiness is a key feature of small streams, in terms of leaf litter and algal mat distributions, and this reflects differences in N\(_2\)-fixation rates across stream compartments. The highest rates of N\(_2\) fixation are often associated with patches of leaf litter and algal mats, and the current study agrees (Henry and Fisher 2003; Marcarelli et al. 2008). Targeted grab samples in our study exhibited the highest rates of N\(_2\) fixation, substantially higher than equivalent amounts of sediments. To better understand the role of N\(_2\) fixation in stream N budgets, coverage estimates for algal mats and leaf litter are needed, but this was not done rigorously in the current study. No significant correlations were observed between N\(_2\)-fixation rates and estimates of fine benthic organic matter or ash-free dry mass (g dry mass m\(^{-2}\)) of leaves, wood, and epilithon (estimates from O’Brien et al. 2007). Samples of algal mats exhibited N\(_2\)-fixation rates some 30-fold greater than in the bottom sediments. Thus, even if only 3% of a basin was covered with algal mats, their contribution to N\(_2\) fixation might equal that of the remaining 97% of the basin comprised of sediments.

At Kings Creek N4D, patches of leaf litter were found to have N\(_2\)-fixation rates that were 4-fold greater than the sediments of this reach. This stream has a cobbled bottom with limited areas of sediment. Seasonal factors and scouring events will have a role in determining the balance between fixation in sediments and leaf litter in streams like Kings Creek. Finally, the concrete basin of Big Blue River Ditch had remarkably productive patches. N\(_2\)-fixation activity was high in algal communities within depressions and grooves in the concrete and in algal streamers attached to the bottom. The patchiness of organisms actively fixing N make whole-stream assessments more difficult especially since the patches are often transient and subject to changes in stream flow, seasons, and nutrient inputs.

The contribution of N\(_2\) fixation to stream N budgets may be more significant in specific patches of streams or in certain streams. Diazotrophs may have a selective advantage in streams with low N loading. The same may be true for microniches where fixed N could be locally limiting, even in bulk sediments that do not appear to be N-limited. Channeling of fixed N compounds from cyanobacteria to attendant bacterial communities is well known (Scott and Marcarelli 2012). The coupling of diazotrophs to symbiotic bacteria (and fungi)

Seasonal variation and cross-shelf distribution of the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium, Trichodesmium, in southern East China Sea Jeng Chang a,*, Kuo-Ping Chiang b, Gwo-Ching Gong c a Institute of Marine Biology, National Taiwan Ocean University, Keelung 202-24, Taiwan, ROC b Department of Fishery Science, National Taiwan Ocean University, Keelung 202-24, Taiwan, ROC c Department of Oceanography, National Taiwan Ocean University, Keelung 202-24, Taiwan, ROC Abstract The abundance of a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium, Trichodesmium, in the southern East China Sea was surveyed along a cross-shelf transect from 1993 to 1996. Trichodesmium existed mostly in surface water between 0 and 50 m depth, with population densities ranging from 0 to 600 trichomes l\(^{-1}\). A clear seasonal cycle was observed in Trichodesmium standing crop which reached more than 10\(^7\) trichomes m\(^{-2}\) in summer and became undetectable in winter. The cross-shelf distribution showed a spring-type pattern with higher abundance in the Kuroshio current and low abundance in the coastal zone. In fall months, a reversed distribution pattern appeared with high abundance in the coastal zone and decreasing concentrations toward the shelf break. These distribution patterns were difficult to be explained by temperature alone, and a coastal substance may be important in determining Trichodesmium distribution in shelf seas. The calculated nitrogen fixation rate of Trichodesmium ranged from 0.1 to 59 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) in the upwelling zone and Kuroshio under non-bloom conditions. This result suggested that Trichodesmium is one of the major contributors to new production in Kuroshio waters. Keywords: Cyanobacterium; East China Sea; Nitrogen fixation; Trichodesmium abundance 1. Introduction Trichodesmium is a filamentous cyanobacterium that inhabits tropical and subtropical seas (for a recent review, see Capone et al., 1997). Trichodesmium is also diazotrophic, a term which depicts its ability to produce ammonium from dinitrogen, and nitrogen fixed via this process supports a significant amount of new production globally (Karl et al., 1997). For example, in the tropical North Atlantic Ocean, Trichodesmium has been shown as the most important new nitrogen source in the euphotic zone (Carpenter and Romans, 1991). At a station in North Pacific Ocean near Hawaii, Trichodesmium supports 27% of the new production under non-bloom conditions (Letelier and Karl, 1996). On the other hand, the importance of Trichodesmium and nitrogen fixation to nutrient dynamics in shelf seas is less clear. According to Trichodesmium abundance and nitrogen fixation rates measured in East China Sea, Saino and Hattori (1980) estimated that 6% of the nitrogen requirement in supporting annual primary production was provided by this cyanobacterium. In addition, shelf seas may receive biologically fixed nitrogen originated from the open ocean. Based on \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) measurements, Liu et al. (1996) estimated that 20% of the nitrate supplied by an upwelling system, which pumped Kuroshio subsurface water to East China Sea, came from nitrogen fixation. An understanding of the distribution of diazotrophic organisms in shelf seas is important to the modeling of nitrogen fixation as well as carbon cycling in these ecosystems. Equipped with buoyancy-regulating gas vesicles and nitrogen fixation enzymes, Trichodesmium is regarded as an organism well adapted to stratified, oligotrophic conditions (Capone et al., 1997). Thus, Trichodesmium abundance should be high in the boundary current and decrease toward the coast as nitrogenous nutrients become more available. Although such a pattern has been regularly observed in the East China Sea during summer months (Marumo and Asaoka, 1974), other distribution patterns do exist. Data presented by Marumo and Asaoka (1974) during one summer cruise revealed a second maximum of Trichodesmium abundance near the coast. In addition, the frequently occurring coastal blooms of this cyanobacterium suggested that it can survive and compete with other phytoplankton in coastal waters (Marumo and Asaoka, 1974; Hong et al., 1992). The interest in studying Trichodesmium distribution also comes from recent reports about harmful blooms of this organism which caused damages to local fish and shellfish populations (Hong et al., 1992). The adverse effects of blooms may be related to several toxins generated by Trichodesmium which are lethal to marine organisms including copepods and mackerel fish (Hawser et al., 1992; Endean et al., 1993). The recognition of environmental conditions that favor bloom formation thus has social and economical implications. In this report, Trichodesmium abundance obtained from 12 cruises along a cross-shelf cruise track in southern East China Sea was analyzed in the hope of understanding spatial and temporal distributions of this organism in shelf seas. From the observed distribution patterns, possible controlling mechanisms were inferred, and estimates were made for the amount of nitrogen fixed by Trichodesmium. 2. Materials and methods A total of 12 cruises were conducted between November 1993 and April 1996 to collect water samples for Trichodesmium enumeration in the southern East China Sea J. Stations off the KEEPKEY transect were visited during the April 1995 (○), the January 1996 (▲), and the April 1996 cruises (△), respectively. Names of the four hydrographic zones used in the text are marked above the corresponding stations. (Table 1). All cruise tracks ran in a cross-shelf direction and were approximately normal to isobaths (Fig. 1). Among them, eight cruises sailed along a transect starting at 26°20′N, 120°30′E and ending at 25°0′N, 123°10′E, and the other four cruises visited stations in the close vicinity. The major transect was named KEEPKEY transect since it has been frequently surveyed during the operation period of the KEEP (Kuroshio Edge Exchange Processes) project. The hydrography along the KEEPKEY transect is fairly well known and several zones can be recognized according to physical and chemical properties of sea water (Gong et al., 1995, 1996). The region between KEEPKEY stations 1 and 3 is the coastal zone, and is typically occupied by the low temperature, low salinity coastal water. Stations 5 and 7 belong to the mid-shelf zone occupied by low nutrient Taiwan Strait water, and stations 9 to 11 are usually occupied by high nutrient water from an upwelling system. The region between stations 15 and 17 is the Kuroshio zone. The euphotic zone in this region is always occupied by warm, nutrient-poor Kuroshio water (Fig. 1). Water samples for Trichodesmium enumeration were collected with a rosette sampler equipped with 2.5 l Go-Flo bottles (General Oceanics, Miami). One liter of sea water was transferred to plastic bottles and fixed immediately with acidic Lugol’s solution (Thronsdon, 1978). In the laboratory, phytoplankton cells in water samples were allowed to settle for at least 48 h and the supernatant was carefully withdrawn by an aspirator until about 50 ml remained in the bottle. The concentrated water sample was then transferred to a conical centrifuge tube and stored in dark at 4°C. Immediately before microscope examination, the sample was concentrated again to a final volume of 1 ml, and loaded to a Sedgwick–Rafter counting cell. The entire counting cell was scanned using a Nikon Optiphot-2 microscope at 100×, and number of trichomes (Trichodesmium filaments) encountered were used to evaluate Trichodesmium abundance. A small fraction of trichomes in our sample were less than 200 μm in length. These short trichomes were excluded in our counts to avoid bias. According to our preliminary experiment (Chang, 1999), Trichodesmium abundance generated this way showed no significant difference from filtering 1 l of sea water onto a Nuclepore filter on deck followed by epi-fluorescent microscope counting. Counting 10 samples repeatedly collected from the same depth at a station revealed that a single-sample estimate should carry a coefficient of variation of 62%. As a result, the present counting method was intended for the detection of abundance differences greater than an order of magnitude. A somewhat different method was adopted to count trichomes in samples from the July cruise in 1994. Samples were settled in 100 ml Utermöhl sedimentation cylinders and counted on a Nikon inverted-microscope (Hasle, 1978). Samples from the KEEPKEY station 1 of the May 1994 cruise have been counted by the Sedgwick–Rafter method and the Utermöhl method, and both methods did not detect any trichomes in the water column. An examination of the abundance of a chain-forming diatom, Rhizosolenia, in the same batch of samples revealed that the difference between these two counting methods ranged from 0 to 200%. Temperature and salinity data were measured with a Seabird CTD (SBE9/11 plus, Seabird Inc. WA). The mixed layer depth was obtained from the upper region on a density profile where the variation in \( \sigma_0 \) was less than 0.16. Chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations were measured in duplicates using a Turner Designs Fluorometer (Model 10-AU-005) according to standard procedures (Parsons et al., 1984). Samples for nutrient determination were quickly frozen in liquid nitrogen and then stored at \( -18^\circ \mathrm{C} \) until analysis. The concentration of nitrate and nitrite were determined by the pink azo dye method, and phosphate were determined by the molybdenum blue method (Parsons et al., 1984; Pai et al., 1990; Gong, 1992). 3. Results In all samples, Trichodesmium mainly appeared as individual trichomes. Colonial forms existed, but were very rare. As a result, attempts were not made to distinguish between various species in this genus. Of all stations visited, Trichodesmium trichomes always existed in the surface layer (Figs. 2(a) and 3(a)). Population densities decreased rapidly when depth became greater than 50 m. A maximum of biomass usually occurred at a depth of 20–30 m. Sometimes, a second maximum appeared near sea surface (Fig. 3(a)). In the Kuroshio, the highest abundance occurred in May 1995, reaching 276 trichomes l\(^{-1}\) at KEEPKEY station 17 (Fig. 2(a)). The abundance was greatly reduced in winter months. At most a few trichomes were found in a liter of sea water. The depth-integrated Trichodesmium abundance showed a clear seasonal cycle with March to May as the growth phase and September to November as the decline phase (Fig. 2(b)). However, the year-to-year variation in Trichodesmium standing crop can not be overlooked. For example, in May 1995, \(10^7\) trichomes m\(^{-2}\) was observed in Kuroshio. In contrast, only \(10^5\) trichomes m\(^{-2}\) was observed at the end of April 1996, a reduction of 100 times (Fig. 2(b)). Environmental factors in Kuroshio possessed a similar seasonal cycle. Water temperature was 24\(^\circ\)C in winter, but increased to 29\(^\circ\)C in summer (Fig. 2(c)). As for mixing strength, strong northeast monsoons in winter generated a mixed layer more than 100 m thick. When weather became more stable in summer, the mixed layer depths were typically around 30 m. The seasonal variation of Trichodesmium standing crop in the upwelling region had a pattern resembling that in the Kuroshio with higher abundance in summer (Fig. 3(b)). The highest population density observed was 600 trichomes l\(^{-1}\). Compared to the seasonal cycle in the Kuroshio, Trichodesmium declined earlier in the upwelling region. Starting from the end of September, no trichomes were detected in this area. The cross-shelf distribution of Trichodesmium revealed different patterns in spring, summer, and fall. In spring, cold water with temperature around 20\(^\circ\)C occupied the area between the coast and the upwelling while Kuroshio water was still warmer than 24\(^\circ\)C (Fig. 4(a)). On the four cruises that covered the KEEPKEY transect in spring months, Trichodesmium was always undetectable in the coastal zone (Fig. 5(a)). However, at a distance of 150–250 km from shore, trichomes started to appear, and population densities increased toward Kuroshio. In contrast, phytoplankton biomass, as indicated by chlorophyll \(a\) concentrations, was constantly low in the Kuroshio (Fig. 4(d)). High levels of chlorophyll were usually observed at the outer fringe of the upwelling, apparently supported by the nutrients supplied from the deep (Figs. 4(b) and (c)). In fall, the difference in temperature between Kuroshio and coastal water was less than 3\(^\circ\) (Fig. 4(a)). A sudden drop near stations 11 to 13 marked the presence of cold Fig. 2. When spring data between 1994 and 1996 were combined, a statistically significant relationship was found between temperature at 10 m depth and integrated Trichodesmium abundance (Fig. 6(a)). The positive correlation existed even when data points with zero value were excluded from the regression. However, temperature alone was unable to explain all distribution patterns observed in the East China Sea. For the fall-type distribution, no relationship with water temperature could be established (Fig. 6(b)). The population density in the Kuroshio was 30 times less than that in the coastal zone while water temperature in Kuroshio remained warmer than 28°C (Figs. 4 and 5). Similarly, temperature alone failed to explain the observed seasonal cycle of Trichodesmium in Kuroshio (Fig. 2). The Kuroshio water near Taiwan is constantly warmer than 24°C year-round. Thus, it is surprising to see that Trichodesmium abundance went through such an dramatic change in a year. Of course, *Trichodesmium*'s ability in fixing nitrogen is vulnerable to turbulence (Carpenter and Price, 1976), and the strong mixing in winter might cause *Trichodesmium* abundance to decrease in the warm Kuroshio (Fig. 2(c)). However, a rapid decrease in *Trichodesmium* abundance was noticed in fall when water temperature was still high and the mixing depth was shallower than 50 m (Fig. 2). Marumo and Asaoka (1974) proposed that a substance in coastal water is essential for the growth of *Trichodesmium*. Because of this substance, dense *Trichodesmium* populations formed at several locations along the course of Kuroshio where the mixing with coastal waters took place (Marumo and Asaoka, 1974). In our study area, the most intensive mixing between the coastal water and the Kuroshio current occurs in winter when part of the Kuroshio flows onto the East China Sea continental shelf (Gong et al., 1997). As a result, ample amount of this substance enters the Kuroshio zone during winter, and supports *Trichodesmium* growth in spring when mixing depth decreases. Later, the active growth in spring and summer deprived this substance from Kuroshio which in turn retarded *Trichodesmium* growth and caused the standing crop to shrink in fall (Figs. 2 and 4). Meanwhile, temperature in the coastal zone was quite warm in fall, and a continuous supply of this substance stimulated the growth of *Trichodesmium*, caused its biomass to increase, and created an environment favoring bloom formation. The phenomenon of a coastal substance in controlling *Trichodesmium* distribution was further supported by observations made on a cruise that covered the entire East China Sea in 1992. High trichome concentrations were mainly found in an area influenced by the Yangtze River (Chen et al., 1996; Gong et al., 1996). However, there is no direct evidence to confirm such a relationship in East China Sea, and other mechanisms, such as the grazing by toxin-resistant harpacticoid copepods (O’Neil and Roman, 1994), cannot be excluded as possible causes for the observed distribution patterns. The amount of new nitrogen introduced to East China Sea and Kuroshio by *Trichodesmium* can be estimated from trichome concentration and nitrogen fixation rate. According to measurements conducted in Kuroshio near southern Japan (Saino and Hattori, 1980), an averaged acetylene reduction rate was 0.7 pmole ethylene trichome\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\) in samples containing only individual trichomes. If we accept the theoretical 3 : 1 acetylene reduction to nitrogen fixation conversion ratio (Capone, 1993), and the fact that *Trichodesmium* fixes nitrogen only in sunlight hours (assumed to be 12 h per day, Saino and Hattori, 1980), nitrogen fixation rate in the Kuroshio/East China Sea region would be 5.6 pmol N trichome\(^{-1}\) d\(^{-1}\). Based on *Trichodesmium* abundance observed at our study area, nitrogen fixation rate in Kuroshio was estimated as between 0.1 and 59 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Table 2). This estimate was extremely close to the 34 \( \pm \) 11 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) nitrogen fixation input required to maintain the depletion of \(^{15}\)N observed at 100 m depth in the same region (Liu et al., 1996). Using the same computational procedure, if *Trichodesmium* nitrogen fixation was not suppressed by the elevated nitrate supply in the upwelling region, the resultant nitrogen input would range from 0.3 to 34 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) (Table 2). Since the f-ratio in Kuroshio ranged from 0.09 to 0.25 (Gong, unpublished), Trichodesmium may contribute up to 25% of the local new production. In contrast, the fraction of primary production supported by nitrogen fixation in the upwelling zone was much less (Table 2). However, because Trichodesmium blooms were never encountered during our survey, the above estimate reflected nitrogen input under non-bloom conditions. Recent evidence indicated that nitrogen fixation rate in a Trichodesmium bloom can reach a very high level at 150 pg N trichome⁻¹ h⁻¹ (129 pmol N trichome⁻¹ d⁻¹), presumably due to colony formation (Carpenter and Capone, 1992). In August 1990, high densities of Trichodesmium at 3.7 × 10⁴ trichomes l⁻¹ was observed at a station in the mid-shelf zone of East China Sea (Chen, 1992). If this bloom extended from sea surface to a depth of merely 1 m, the depth-integrated biomass would reach 3.7 × 10⁷ trichomes m⁻². When the nitrogen fixation rate under bloom condition was applied, Trichodesmium would support a primary productivity of 31.5 mmol C m⁻² d⁻¹, much higher than total primary productivity normally measured in the Kuroshio zone. Seasonal variation and cross-shelf distribution of the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium, Trichodesmium, in southern East China Sea

Jeng Chang a,*, Kuo-Ping Chiang b, Gwo-Ching Gong c

a Institute of Marine Biology, National Taiwan Ocean University, Keelung 202-24, Taiwan, ROC
b Department of Fishery Science, National Taiwan Ocean University, Keelung 202-24, Taiwan, ROC
c Department of Oceanography, National Taiwan Ocean University, Keelung 202-24, Taiwan, ROC

Abstract

The abundance of a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium, Trichodesmium, in the southern East China Sea was surveyed along a cross-shelf transect from 1993 to 1996. Trichodesmium existed mostly in surface water between 0 and 50 m depth, with population densities ranging from 0 to 600 trichomes l\(^{-1}\). A clear seasonal cycle was observed in Trichodesmium standing crop which reached more than 10\(^7\) trichomes m\(^{-2}\) in summer and became undetectable in winter. The cross-shelf distribution showed a spring-type pattern with higher abundance in the Kuroshio current and low abundance in the coastal zone. In fall months, a reversed distribution pattern appeared with high abundance in the coastal zone and decreasing concentrations toward the shelf break. These distribution patterns were difficult to be explained by temperature alone, and a coastal substance may be important in determining Trichodesmium distribution in shelf seas. The calculated nitrogen fixation rate of Trichodesmium ranged from 0.1 to 59 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) in the upwelling zone and Kuroshio under non-bloom conditions. This result suggested that Trichodesmium is one of the major contributors to new production in Kuroshio waters.

Keywords: Cyanobacterium; East China Sea; Nitrogen fixation; Trichodesmium abundance

1. Introduction

Trichodesmium is a filamentous cyanobacterium that inhabits tropical and subtropical seas (for a recent review, see Capone et al., 1997). Trichodesmium is also diazotrophic,

Of course, *Trichodesmium*'s ability in fixing nitrogen is vulnerable to turbulence (Carpenter and Price, 1976), and the strong mixing in winter might cause *Trichodesmium* abundance to decrease in the warm Kuroshio (Fig. 2(c)). However, a rapid decrease in *Trichodesmium* abundance was noticed in fall when water temperature was still high and the mixing depth was shallower than 50 m (Fig. 2).

Marumo and Asaoka (1974) proposed that a substance in coastal water is essential for the growth of *Trichodesmium*. Because of this substance, dense *Trichodesmium* populations formed at several locations along the course of Kuroshio where the mixing with coastal waters took place (Marumo and Asaoka, 1974). In our study area, the most intensive mixing between the coastal water and the Kuroshio current occurs in winter when part of the Kuroshio flows onto the East China Sea continental shelf (Gong et al., 1997). As a result, ample amount of this substance enters the Kuroshio zone during winter, and supports *Trichodesmium* growth in spring when mixing depth decreases. Later, the active growth in spring and summer deprived this substance from Kuroshio which in turn retarded *Trichodesmium* growth and caused the standing crop to shrink in fall (Figs. 2 and 4). Meanwhile, temperature in the coastal zone was quite warm in fall, and a continuous supply of this substance stimulated the growth of *Trichodesmium*, caused its biomass to increase, and created an environment favoring bloom formation. The phenomenon of a coastal substance in controlling *Trichodesmium* distribution was further supported by observations made on a cruise that covered the entire East China Sea in 1992. High trichome concentrations were mainly found in an area influenced by the Yangtze River (Chen et al., 1996; Gong et al., 1996). However, there is no direct evidence to confirm such a relationship in East China Sea, and other mechanisms, such as the grazing by toxin-resistant harpacticoid copepods (O’Neil and Roman, 1994), cannot be excluded as possible causes for the observed distribution patterns.

The amount of new nitrogen introduced to East China Sea and Kuroshio by *Trichodesmium* can be estimated from trichome concentration and nitrogen fixation rate. According to measurements conducted in Kuroshio near southern Japan (Saino and Hattori, 1980), an averaged acetylene reduction rate was 0.7 pmole ethylene trichome\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\) in samples containing only individual trichomes. If we accept the theoretical 3 : 1 acetylene reduction to nitrogen fixation conversion ratio (Capone, 1993), and the fact that *Trichodesmium* fixes nitrogen only in sunlight hours (assumed to be 12 h per day, Saino and Hattori, 1980), nitrogen fixation rate in the Kuroshio/East China Sea region would be 5.6 pmol N trichome\(^{-1}\) d\(^{-1}\). Based on *Trichodesmium* abundance observed at our study area, nitrogen fixation rate in Kuroshio was estimated as between 0.1 and 59 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Table 2). This estimate was extremely close to the 34 \( \pm \) 11 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) nitrogen fixation input required to maintain the depletion of \(^{15}\)N observed at 100 m depth in the same region (Liu et al., 1996). Using the same computational procedure, if *Trichodesmium* nitrogen fixation was not suppressed by the elevated nitrate supply in the upwelling region, the resultant nitrogen input would range from 0.3 to 34 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) (Table 2).

Epiphytic Nitrogen Fixation Associated With Standing Dead Shoots of Smooth Cordgrass, Spartina alterniflora CAROLYN A. CURRIN1 National Marine Fisheries Service National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Beaufort Laboratory 101 Pivers Island Road Beaufort, North Carolina 28516 HANS W. PAERL University of North Carolina Institute of Marine Sciences Morehead City, North Carolina 28516 ABSTRACT: N_2 fixation associated with the epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora shoots was examined in both a natural and transplanted salt marsh in North Carolina. Acetylene reduction (AR) assays were conducted over a 24-mo period to estimate N_2 fixation rates on standing dead stems and leaves. In the natural salt marsh, mean AR rates ranged from 0.5 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 14 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, while in the transplanted marsh mean AR rates ranged from 1 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 33 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}. Diel AR activity of epiphytic communities in both marshes varied seasonally. Midday incubations yielded higher AR rates than nighttime incubations in the spring, while midday incubations in late summer and fall generally yielded AR rates equal to or lower than nighttime incubations. Desiccation during low tides occasionally repressed AR activity, although AR rates quickly rebounded with wetting. AR activity was localized in the epiphytic community, rather than in the underlying Spartina stem material. Based on the measured AR rates and the density of standing dead stems, the annual input of new N to the natural salt marsh via epiphytic N_2 fixation is estimated to be 2.6 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. The estimate of annual input of new N to the transplanted marsh is 3.8 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. These estimates should be added to previous estimates of N_2 fixation in marsh sediments to estimate the total contribution of new nitrogen to salt marsh nitrogen budgets. Introduction Salt marsh primary production is often limited by the availability of fixed nitrogen (Valiela 1983). Accordingly, there have been numerous efforts to quantify the amount of new N added to salt marsh ecosystems via N_2 fixation (Valiela 1983; Capone 1985; Howarth et al. 1988). The majority of previous studies have focused on sedimentary N_2 fixation, including surface and subsurface sediments, and rhizospheric N_2 fixation associated with live Spartina alterniflora. Epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina stems and leaves has also been recorded (Green and Edmisten 1974; Hanson 1977; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981; Talbot et al. 1988; Newell et al. 1992). Of these studies, three provide estimates of the annual N input from epiphytic N_2 fixation, which vary by over two orders of magnitude. Two lower estimates are from Georgia and Louisiana salt marshes, where epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina leaves and stems was estimated to yield 0.47 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} and 0.66 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}, respectively (Hanson 1977; Casselman et al. 1981). In a Florida salt marsh, epiphytic N_2 fixation was estimated to yield 287 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} (Green and Edmisten 1974, but see Newell et al. 1992). The Louisiana and Georgia epiphytic communities were dominated by diatoms and eukaryotic, filamentous and coccoid algae. Cyanobacteria represented an average of 4% of the total epiphytic biovolume in Georgia (Fallon et al. 1985), and were absent from the Louisiana epiphytic community (Day et al. 1973). Two genera of N_2-fixing bacteria (Rhodospirillum and Rhodopseudomonas) were cultured from the epiphytic community examined in Florida, while cyanobacteria were only isolated from sediment samples (Green and Edmisten 1974). The epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora in North Carolina salt marshes includes cyanobacteria (Calothrix spp. and Lyngbya spp. were dominant), diatoms, green algae, and heterotrophic and photosynthetic bacteria (Currin and Paerl 1997). Results from diel experiments suggest that N_2 fixation in this community is light-dependent, and that cyanobacteria are the microorganisms primarily responsible for the observed N_2-fixing activity. On an areal basis, estimated daily N_2 fixation rates (acetylene reduction assays) on standing dead Spartina stems were as high as 50 mg N m^{-2} d^{-1} (Currin and Paerl 1997), comparable to the highest rates recorded from other salt marsh environments (Capone 1983, 1985). Environmental factors controlling epiphytic N_2 fixation have been examined utilizing standing dead leaves and stems collected from Sapelo Island, Georgia (Newell et al. 1992). In that study, N_2 fixation rates as estimated by acetylene reduction (AR) assays were lowest during the winter on leaves with low ash content (<15%), while leaves collected May–August contained a higher ash content (>40%) and exhibited AR rates that were 10 times higher than the winter AR rates. Standing dead stems and leaves demonstrated similar AR rates on an ash-free dry weight (AFDW) basis. Newly senescent leaves had very low AR rates until 4 wk after tagging, and AR rates continued to rise throughout the 12-wk period after tagging. Other investigators have also documented higher rates of AR on dead stems than on live stems (Green and Edmisten 1974; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981). The objectives of this research were to determine seasonal patterns in AR rates associated with standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems collected from both a mature, natural salt marsh and a transplanted salt marsh. Although results from diel experiments strongly implicated epiphytic cyanobacteria as the primary N_2-fixing microorganisms on standing dead Spartina stems (Currin and Paerl 1997), separate incubations of the epiphytic film and underlying stem were made to determine the physical location of the N_2-fixing activity. In addition, the effects of desiccation, ash content, and shoot part (stem versus leaf) on AR rates were examined. An estimate of the annual N input by the epiphytic community is made for both a mature, natural marsh and a young (<3 yr old), transplanted marsh. Materials and Methods Standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems were collected from adjacent natural and transplanted marshes in the Newport River Estuary, North Carolina. The created marsh was planted with Spartina alterniflora in June 1990 (Currin et al. 1996). Collections from the natural marsh were made from five sites in a transect extending from a short Spartina zone (one site), through tall Spartina (two sites), and ending in another short Spartina zone (two sites) in the upper intertidal. Spartina stems were also collected from five sites established in the transplanted marsh, which included tall-form and short-form Spartina zones. A survey of the marshes demonstrated that there is <0.3 m difference in tidal elevation among all of the collection sites (C. Currin unpublished data). Standing dead stems were defined as the stem portion of Spartina shoots that is yellow-brown to brown in color, may include old sheaths but not blades, and remains upright on the marsh surface. Stems were chosen either randomly, using quadrants and random numbers, or arbitrarily with no selection criteria other than that described above. On several occasions, newly senescent stems (yellow-brown color, leaves intact, height >40 cm) were distinguished from old dead stems (brown color, leaves absent, height <25 cm). For AR assays (described below), 4-cm stem sections were removed from the zone between 5 cm and 15 cm from the base of the stem. Sample collections in the adjacent natural marsh were made in April, June, and October 1991; August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May, and June 1993. Samples were collected from the transplanted marsh in April and October 1991; February, August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May and June 1993. Additionally, results from submerged and aerial incubations from diel experiments run in March, July, and October 1992 and May 1993 (Currin and Paerl 1997) were included in estimates of annual N_2 fixation rates. The majority of incubations were done at midday (MD), defined as the period 1100–1500 hours. Incubations designated as evening (PM) were begun at or shortly after sunset (1730–2030 hours). Incubations designated as morning (AM) were begun near sunrise (0545–0800 hours). AR assays were used to estimate N_2 fixation rates (Hardy et al. 1968). All incubations were done in air, with the exception of submerged incubations in diel experiments (see Currin and Paerl 1997). After immersion in seawater (30–35%o) for 5 s, a 4-cm stem section was placed in a clean (HCl-soaked, distilled water rinsed) glass 38-ml serum bottle sealed with a rubber stopper. Seven ml of the headspace was withdrawn with a syringe, and replaced with 7.4 ml of CaC_2-generated acetylene. Bottles were incubated upright in a running water bath at ambient temperatures, when possible. Many of the incubations were done in the field, without access to running water, and so the bath water was changed periodically to minimize temperature changes. After a 2–3 h incubation, assays were terminated by injecting 9 ml distilled water, mixing, and withdrawing 9 ml of the headspace to an evacuated 9.6-ml serum bottle. The ethylene content of the headspace was determined by injecting 0.3-ml subsamples into a Shimadzu GC 8A gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector and a Poropak T column maintained at 80°C. N2 served as the carrier gas, and ethylene concentrations were determined by comparisons to standards prepared from pure ethylene (Matheson Gas Company). Upon termination of the AR assay, stems were removed from sample bottles and stem length and diameter recorded. Acetylene reduction rates are reported on a cm^2 basis, reflecting the stem surface area. In some instances, stem dry mass and organic matter content were obtained by drying for 48 h at 95°C, followed by ashing for 8 h at 500°C. The effect of desiccation on stem AR rates was examined on four occasions in September 1992 and once in December 1992. In the first experiment, stems from both marshes were collected during low and high tide periods of two consecutive tidal cycles, and incubated without any pretreatment (i.e., no seawater submergence). In subsequent experiments, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes ca. 60 min after slack low tide. Half of the stems from each marsh were immersed in seawater prior to AR assay (standard protocol), while the other half were placed in incubation bottles without the seawater immersion pretreatment. AR incubations were otherwise as described above. The potential locus of standing dead stem N2 fixation was determined in June 1991 and December 1992 by dissecting the epiphytic film away from the stem, and assaying both portions for AR. In June, 10 stems were collected from the natural marsh, and five stems were divided into epiphytic film and underlying stem portions. Dissection was done using a scalpel, and some fibrous Spartina material was retained in the epiphytic film. The remaining five stems were incubated intact. In December, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes and were treated as in June. Leaf blades attached to standing dead stems were assayed for AR on four occasions. The first or second leaf closest to the stem base was collected from the transplanted marsh in February, May, November, and December. Similar collections were made in the natural marsh in May and November. Leaves were immersed for 5 s in seawater prior to AR assay and treated as described above for stem incubations. The density of standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems was measured twice in the course of this study. On each occasion, 0.0625-m^2 quadrats were located randomly adjacent to the transects normally sampled for stem collections. The number of standing dead stems was measured in 10 replicate quadrats in each marsh. Statistical analysis was conducted with SAS software (SAS Institute Co., Cary North Carolina). One-way analysis of variance was used to determine significance of effects when class variables had three or more levels, and Tukey's test was used to determine the significance of differences between selected treatment means. Pairwise comparisons were done with t-tests. Data were log-transformed when necessary (fmax test), and significance was determined at p < 0.05. Results AR Rates in Natural and Transplanted Marshes There was no significant difference in AR rates (nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) between newly senescent and old standing stems in either marsh at any sampling time (t-test, p > 0.05). Therefore, data from senescent and old stems are combined in subsequent analyses. Leaves collected from standing dead stems in the natural and transplanted marshes had AR rates similar to stems, both on an areal (cm^2) and ash-free dry weight basis (p > 0.05). The only exception to this occurred in May 1993 when transplanted marsh stems had AR rates (4.26 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) which were significantly higher than AR rates on leaves (1.31 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, t-test, p < 0.01). On an ash-free dry weight basis, however, standing dead stem and leaf AR rates were not significantly different at any sampling time. The average AR activity on standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems incubated at midday ranged from <1 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} in the natural marsh during November and December to 17 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} on stems collected from the transplanted marsh in July (Table 1; Fig. 1). Midday AR rates were significantly higher than morning or evening AR rates in December and May in the transplanted marsh and in March in the natural marsh. However, in the period July to October, midday AR incubations were equal to or significantly lower than morning or evening incubations (Fig. 1). On most sampling days, AR rates associated with standing dead stems from the natural marsh were equal to or lower than rates associated with stems from the transplanted marsh. The most distinct break in this pattern occurred in April 1991, when AR rates on stems from the natural marsh were significantly higher than those from the transplanted marsh (ANOVA, p < 0.05). This occurred on the first sampling date, after only one growing season, and was the only occasion when well-developed epiphytic films were not observed in the transplanted marsh. Data from dates on which both natural and transplanted marshes were sampled were used to determine whether marsh type had a significant effect on AR rates (April and October 1991; August, September, November, and December 1992; January, March, and May 1993). The mean AR rates of each marsh type on the selected dates were compared using one-way analysis of variance. This reduced the degrees of freedom but avoided invalid assumptions due to an unbalanced dataset. This conservative approach does not reject the null hypothesis (p = 0.067). As noted above, April 1991 differed from all other sampling dates in that, after only one growing season, no epiphytic films were observed on transplanted marsh stems. Excluding this point from the analysis results in a significant difference in epiphytic AR rates between the natural and transplanted marsh (p = 0.013, 25 d.f.). There also appears to be a temporal pattern in the difference in AR rates between the two marshes. Mean AR rates are most similar from December to June. Mean AR rates are most dissimilar from July to November, when standing dead stems in the transplanted marsh may exhibit AR rates 2–5 times higher than natural marsh stems. DESICCATION EFFECTS In September, exposed stems collected at an early morning low tide, and incubated aerially without prior wetting, exhibited measurable AR rates that were comparable to rates measured on submerged stems collected at the next high tide and incubated aerially (Fig. 2). However, exposed stems collected during the afternoon low tide were visibly more desiccated than the early morning exposed stems, and did not exhibit measurable AR activity. Stems collected at the next high tide had completely recovered AR activity (Fig. 2). Measurable AR activity was detected on exposed, unwetted stems collected from both marshes on four other dates (Fig. 3a,b). In the natural marsh, AR rates associated with exposed, unwetted stems were not significantly different from exposed, wetted stems on any occasion (t-test, p > 0.05). Exposed stems from the transplanted marsh which were wetted prior to incubation always had higher AR rates than unwetted stems, although the differences were significant (p < 0.05) on only two occasions (September 16 and December 9; Fig. 4b). Variability in AR rates was particularly high in these experiments, with the average coefficient of variation equal to 70%. CHARACTERISTICS OF STANDING DEAD MATERIAL The contribution of the epiphytic film to standing dead stem N2 fixation was evaluated in June and December. In June, there was no significant difference in AR rates (nmol C2H4 4-cm section−1 h−1) between intact stems and epiphytic films removed from the stem (ANOVA, p > 0.05) (Fig. 4). However, stems from which the epiphytic film had been removed had significantly lower AR rates (p < 0.05). In December, similar results were obtained, although the differences were only significant for samples from the transplanted marsh (Fig. 4). Discussion Barring physical perturbation, Spartina alterniflora plants undergo a period of aerial senescence and decomposition after the growing season. In ice-free marshes, standing dead stems may persist for a year or more after senescence, while in more northern latitudes the aerial senescent-decomposition period may be shortened if ice cover pushes stems to the sediment surface. Several previous investigations have demonstrated that standing dead Spartina shoots support greater epiphytic N2 fixation than live shoots (Green and Edmisten 1974; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981). The only critical examination of the relationship between plant senescence and epiphytic N2 fixation was a study by Newell et al. (1992), in which epiphytic N2 fixation rates associated with leaves became detectable 2 wk after senescence, and continued to increase over a 12-wk period. In our study, newly senescent stems, which still retained their upper leaves, did not have significantly different AR rates than older standing dead stems. These observations suggest that not only does epiphytic colonization begin shortly before or just after plant senescence, but that epiphytic N2 fixation rates do not decrease as shoot decomposition progresses. On an areal basis, rates of N₂ fixation by the epiphytic microbial community on standing dead Spartina stems in this study ranged from 1 nmol C₂H₄ cm⁻² h⁻¹ to 30 nmol C₂H₄ cm⁻² h⁻¹ (Table 1). These estimates are comparable to published values of N₂ fixation in salt marsh surface sediments (Jones 1974; Hanson 1977; Carpenter et al. 1978; Patriquin and Denike 1978; Casselman et al. 1981; Currin et al. 1996). Our finding of higher N₂ fixation rates associated with the epiphytic community in the transplanted marsh than the natural marsh is consistent with previous results demonstrating higher rates of N₂ fixation in transplanted marsh sediments than natural marsh sediments (Currin et al. 1996). For the months in which we have no data for nighttime fixation, we assumed that from December to May nighttime N₂ fixation proceeded at half the daytime rate, and that in the period July–November nighttime N₂ fixation proceeded at a rate equal to the daytime rate (Fig. 1). In the natural marsh, the estimated annual N input is 2.5 g N m−2 stem surface yr−1. These community N2 fixation rates are comparable to annual N inputs from intertidal benthic cyanobacterial mats (Capone 1983). The areal extent of the epiphytic film on standing dead stems varies considerably from stem to stem, but usually occurs on most of the lower 20 cm of the stem and on any leaves attached to that part of the stem. Assuming 20 cm of stem with 0.5 cm diameter, plus an additional 5 cm length of leaf, the average epiphyte coverage per standing dead stem is 39 cm2. Further, assuming standing dead stem densities of 150 stems m−2 in the transplanted marsh and 265 stems m−2 in the adjacent natural marsh, estimated N2 fixation by the epiphytic film on stems would be 3.8 g N m−2 marsh surface yr−1 in the transplanted marsh and 2.6 g N m−2 marsh surface yr−1 in the natural marsh. However, most rhizospheric AR assays exhibit a considerable lag time before enzyme activity is measurable (several hours to days), and the above estimates have been criticized as probably being overestimates by as much as an order of magnitude (Howarth et al. 1988). The AR assays conducted in this study to estimate N\(_2\) fixation associated with standing dead Spartina stems lasted 2–3 h and did not display a lag period; nor did those reported by Newell et al. (1992). Seasonal shifts in the N\(_2\)-fixing community, resulting in changes in diel patterns of N\(_2\) fixation, have been reported from several benthic marine habitats (Paerl et al. 1994; Pinckney et al. 1995). The seasonal patterns in day-night N\(_2\) fixation that we observed are similar to those that occur on surface sediments on North Carolina intertidal flats (Pinckney et al. 1995). On standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems, higher midday AR rates in the spring are attributed to the N\(_2\)-fixing activity of heterocystous cyanobacteria, primarily Calothrix spp. (Curran and Paerl 1997). It appears that a spring bloom of heterocystous or coccoid cyanobacteria occurs in both marshes, as epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation rates are similar in early spring incubations. However, during late summer and early fall, epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation in the transplanted marsh is greater than in the natural marsh. One possible explanation is that light becomes limiting in the natural marsh as the Spartina canopy develops. Stem density and biomass was greater in the natural marsh than in the transplanted marsh during this study (Table 2; S. Broome unpublished data), and stem biomass is directly related to canopy light attenuation (Morris 1989). The potential inhibitory effect of desiccation on AR rates was not accounted for in the annual estimates of N\(_2\) fixation reported here. However, the data suggest that exposure, or emergence, inhibits AR rates only during extreme low tides, and that periods of emergence during low tide periods do not necessarily correspond with decreased epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation rates (Figs. 2 and 3). When desiccation does cause a decrease in AR activity, the activity is restored immediately after resubmergence (Fig. 2). Other studies of intertidal microalgal communities have also demonstrated that these microorganisms are resilient following desiccation. Jones (1980) examined the effect of desiccation on photosynthetic CO\(_2\) fixation by the epiphytic community on standing dead stems in a Georgia salt marsh, and determined that even severely desiccated stems recover CO\(_2\) fixation immediately after wetting. Similarly, Jones (1974) and Pulich and Rabalais (1987) found that desiccated intertidal ben- thic cyanobacteria responded almost immediately to the addition of water by resuming N\(_2\) fixation rates comparable to submerged specimens. Apart from any inhibitory effects on epiphytic growth or activity, desiccation probably plays an important role in maintaining the species composition of the epiphytic community on standing dead stems. Calothrix, the dominant cyanobacterial genus in most sampling periods (Curran and Paerl 1997), is often restricted to the upper intertidal in marine environments (Hanson 1977; Javor and Castenholz 1981; Stal et al. 1994), and was never identified in the surface sediment of the marshes we sampled (Curran et al. 1996). In a review of aquatic N\(_2\) fixation, Howarth et al. (1988) suggested that this process was unimportant to salt marsh N budgets, because the amount of N fixed in salt marsh sediments was less than 10% of the total N input. The calculated annual contribution of new N fixed by epiphytic communities on standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems in this study (2–4 g N m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\)) represents an amount almost equal to the total marsh sedimentary N\(_2\) fixation calculated by Howarth et al. (1988) (2–8 g N m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\)), in effect nearly doubling the estimated amount of annual marsh N\(_2\) fixation. In contrast to N fixed in the rhizosphere, epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation is probably of little direct benefit to Spartina. However, its potential importance to grazers and salt marsh nutrient cycles is not trivial. The epiphytic community provides a source of new nitrogen which may be utilized by marsh consumers, or exported from the marsh as dissolved or particulate organic N. In addition, nitrogen fixed by epiphytic microorganisms may become incorporated into standing dead Spartina tissue via fungal or bacterial activity, increasing the N content of aboveground Spartina detritus. White and Howes (1994) calculated that over half of the N in standing dead Spartina tissue is derived from external sources, and suggested that N\(_2\)-fixing microorganisms may contribute new N to detrital Spartina. Similarly, the \(^{15}\)N values of standing dead Spartina tissue collected from the North Carolina marshes examined in this study indicated that microbial N\(_2\) fixation supplied N which was incorporated into detrital Spartina tissue (Curran et al. 1995). Epiphytic microalgae and the associated microbial community may be an important, although often overlooked, food resource for marsh consumers. Multiple stable isotope analysis demonstrated the role of N\(_2\)-fixing cyanobacteria in the food webs of several marsh consumers (Littorina, Uca, Fundulus spp.) in North Carolina marshes (Curran et al. 1995). Other studies have described a diverse meiofaunal community associated with algal epiphytes on Spartina stems, and the utilization of stem-dwelling meiofauna by shrimp and fish (Rutledge and Fleeger 1993; Walters et al. 1996; Gregg and Fleeger in review). Results from this study and from Newell et al. (1992) demonstrate that active N_2-fixing communities develop on standing dead Spartina stems and leaves, and that these communities can differ markedly in species composition. Further research is necessary to determine how widespread these epiphytic communities are in North American Spartina marshes, and to delineate environmental controls on their development, community composition, and N_2-fixing potential. Epiphytic Nitrogen Fixation Associated With Standing Dead Shoots of Smooth Cordgrass, Spartina alterniflora

CAROLYN A. CURRIN1
National Marine Fisheries Service
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
Beaufort Laboratory
101 Pivers Island Road
Beaufort, North Carolina 28516

HANS W. PAERL
University of North Carolina
Institute of Marine Sciences
Morehead City, North Carolina 28516

ABSTRACT: N_2 fixation associated with the epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora shoots was examined in both a natural and transplanted salt marsh in North Carolina. Acetylene reduction (AR) assays were conducted over a 24-mo period to estimate N_2 fixation rates on standing dead stems and leaves. In the natural salt marsh, mean AR rates ranged from 0.5 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 14 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, while in the transplanted marsh mean AR rates ranged from 1 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 33 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}. Diel AR activity of epiphytic communities in both marshes varied seasonally. Midday incubations yielded higher AR rates than nighttime incubations in the spring, while midday incubations in late summer and fall generally yielded AR rates equal to or lower than nighttime incubations. Desiccation during low tides occasionally repressed AR activity, although AR rates quickly rebounded with wetting. AR activity was localized in the epiphytic community, rather than in the underlying Spartina stem material. Based on the measured AR rates and the density of standing dead stems, the annual input of new N to the natural salt marsh via epiphytic N_2 fixation is estimated to be 2.6 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. The estimate of annual input of new N to the transplanted marsh is 3.8 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. These estimates should be added to previous estimates of N_2 fixation in marsh sediments to estimate the total contribution of new nitrogen to salt marsh nitrogen budgets.

Introduction

Salt marsh primary production is often limited by the availability of fixed nitrogen (Valiela 1983). Accordingly, there have been numerous efforts to quantify the amount of new N added to salt marsh ecosystems via N_2 fixation (Valiela 1983; Capone 1985; Howarth et al. 1988). The majority of previous studies have focused on sedimentary N_2 fixation, including surface and subsurface sediments, and rhizospheric N_2 fixation associated with live Spartina alterniflora. Epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina stems and leaves has also been recorded (Green and Edmisten 1974; Hanson 1977; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981; Talbot et al. 1988; Newell et al. 1992). Of these studies, three provide estimates of the annual N input from epiphytic N_2 fixation, which vary by over two orders of magnitude. Two lower estimates are from Georgia and Louisiana salt marshes, where epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina leaves and stems was estimated to yield 0.47 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} and 0.66 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}, respectively (Hanson 1977; Casselman et al. 1981). In a Florida salt marsh, epiphytic N_2 fixation was estimated to yield 287 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} (Green and Edmisten 1974, but see Newell et al. 1992). The Louisiana and Georgia epiphytic communities were dominated by diatoms and eukaryotic, filamentous and coccoid algae. Cyanobacteria represented an average of 4% of the total epiphytic biovolume in Georgia (Fallon et al. 1985), and were absent from the Louisiana epiphytic community (Day et al. 1973). Two genera of N_2-fixing bacteria (Rhodospirillum and Rhodopseudomonas) were cultured from the epiphytic community examined in Florida, while cyanobacteria were only isolated from sediment samples (Green and Edmisten 1974).

The epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora in North Carolina salt marshes includes cyanobacteria (Calothrix spp. and Lyngbya spp. were dominant), diatoms, green algae, and heterotrophic and photosynthetic bacteria (Currin and Paerl 1997). Results from diel experiments
pages.1:
suggest that N_2 fixation in this community is light-dependent, and that cyanobacteria are the microorganisms primarily responsible for the observed N_2-fixing activity. On an areal basis, estimated daily N_2 fixation rates (acetylene reduction assays) on standing dead Spartina stems were as high as 50 mg N m^{-2} d^{-1} (Currin and Paerl 1997), comparable to the highest rates recorded from other salt marsh environments (Capone 1983, 1985).

Environmental factors controlling epiphytic N_2 fixation have been examined utilizing standing dead leaves and stems collected from Sapelo Island, Georgia (Newell et al. 1992). In that study, N_2 fixation rates as estimated by acetylene reduction (AR) assays were lowest during the winter on leaves with low ash content (<15%), while leaves collected May–August contained a higher ash content (>40%) and exhibited AR rates that were 10 times higher than the winter AR rates. Standing dead stems and leaves demonstrated similar AR rates on an ash-free dry weight (AFDW) basis. Newly senescent leaves had very low AR rates until 4 wk after tagging, and AR rates continued to rise throughout the 12-wk period after tagging. Other investigators have also documented higher rates of AR on dead stems than on live stems (Green and Edmisten 1974; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981).

The objectives of this research were to determine seasonal patterns in AR rates associated with standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems collected from both a mature, natural salt marsh and a transplanted salt marsh. Although results from diel experiments strongly implicated epiphytic cyanobacteria as the primary N_2-fixing microorganisms on standing dead Spartina stems (Currin and Paerl 1997), separate incubations of the epiphytic film and underlying stem were made to determine the physical location of the N_2-fixing activity. In addition, the effects of desiccation, ash content, and shoot part (stem versus leaf) on AR rates were examined. An estimate of the annual N input by the epiphytic community is made for both a mature, natural marsh and a young (<3 yr old), transplanted marsh.

Materials and Methods

Standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems were collected from adjacent natural and transplanted marshes in the Newport River Estuary, North Carolina. The created marsh was planted with Spartina alterniflora in June 1990 (Currin et al. 1996). Collections from the natural marsh were made from five sites in a transect extending from a short Spartina zone (one site), through tall Spartina (two sites), and ending in another short Spartina zone (two sites) in the upper intertidal. Spartina stems were also collected from five sites established in the transplanted marsh, which included tall-form and short-form Spartina zones. A survey of the marshes demonstrated that there is <0.3 m difference in tidal elevation among all of the collection sites (C. Currin unpublished data). Standing dead stems were defined as the stem portion of Spartina shoots that is yellow-brown to brown in color, may include old sheaths but not blades, and remains upright on the marsh surface. Stems were chosen either randomly, using quadrants and random numbers, or arbitrarily with no selection criteria other than that described above. On several occasions, newly senescent stems (yellow-brown color, leaves intact, height >40 cm) were distinguished from old dead stems (brown color, leaves absent, height <25 cm). For AR assays (described below), 4-cm stem sections were removed from the zone between 5 cm and 15 cm from the base of the stem.

Sample collections in the adjacent natural marsh were made in April, June, and October 1991; August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May, and June 1993. Samples were collected from the transplanted marsh in April and October 1991; February, August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May and June 1993. Additionally, results from submerged and aerial incubations from diel experiments run in March, July, and October 1992 and May 1993 (Currin and Paerl 1997) were included in estimates of annual N_2 fixation rates. The majority of incubations were done at midday (MD), defined as the period 1100–1500 hours. Incubations designated as evening (PM) were begun at or shortly after sunset (1730–2030 hours). Incubations designated as morning (AM) were begun near sunrise (0545–0800 hours).

AR assays were used to estimate N_2 fixation rates (Hardy et al. 1968). All incubations were done in air, with the exception of submerged incubations in diel experiments (see Currin and Paerl 1997). After immersion in seawater (30–35%o) for 5 s, a 4-cm stem section was placed in a clean (HCl-soaked, distilled water rinsed) glass 38-ml serum bottle sealed with a rubber stopper. Seven ml of the headspace was withdrawn with a syringe, and replaced with 7.4 ml of CaC_2-generated acetylene. Bottles were incubated upright in a running water bath at ambient temperatures, when possible. Many of the incubations were done in the field, without access to running water, and so the bath water was changed periodically to minimize temperature changes. After a 2–3 h incubation, assays were terminated by injecting 9 ml distilled water, mixing, and withdrawing 9 ml of the headspace to an evacuated 9.6-ml serum bottle. The ethylene

content of the headspace was determined by injecting 0.3-ml subsamples into a Shimadzu GC 8A gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector and a Poropak T column maintained at 80°C. N2 served as the carrier gas, and ethylene concentrations were determined by comparisons to standards prepared from pure ethylene (Matheson Gas Company).

Upon termination of the AR assay, stems were removed from sample bottles and stem length and diameter recorded. Acetylene reduction rates are reported on a cm^2 basis, reflecting the stem surface area. In some instances, stem dry mass and organic matter content were obtained by drying for 48 h at 95°C, followed by ashing for 8 h at 500°C.

The effect of desiccation on stem AR rates was examined on four occasions in September 1992 and once in December 1992. In the first experiment, stems from both marshes were collected during low and high tide periods of two consecutive tidal cycles, and incubated without any pretreatment (i.e., no seawater submergence). In subsequent experiments, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes ca. 60 min after slack low tide. Half of the stems from each marsh were immersed in seawater prior to AR assay (standard protocol), while the other half were placed in incubation bottles without the seawater immersion pretreatment. AR incubations were otherwise as described above.

The potential locus of standing dead stem N2 fixation was determined in June 1991 and December 1992 by dissecting the epiphytic film away from the stem, and assaying both portions for AR. In June, 10 stems were collected from the natural marsh, and five stems were divided into epiphytic film and underlying stem portions. Dissection was done using a scalpel, and some fibrous Spartina material was retained in the epiphytic film. The remaining five stems were incubated intact. In December, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes and were treated as in June.

Leaf blades attached to standing dead stems were assayed for AR on four occasions. The first or second leaf closest to the stem base was collected from the transplanted marsh in February, May, November, and December. Similar collections were made in the natural marsh in May and November. Leaves were immersed for 5 s in seawater prior to AR assay and treated as described above for stem incubations.

The density of standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems was measured twice in the course of this study. On each occasion, 0.0625-m^2 quadrats were located randomly adjacent to the transects normally sampled for stem collections. The number of standing dead stems was measured in 10 replicate quadrats in each marsh.

Statistical analysis was conducted with SAS software (SAS Institute Co., Cary North Carolina). One-way analysis of variance was used to determine significance of effects when class variables had three or more levels, and Tukey's test was used to determine the significance of differences between selected treatment means. Pairwise comparisons were done with t-tests. Data were log-transformed when necessary (fmax test), and significance was determined at p < 0.05.

Results

AR Rates in Natural and Transplanted Marshes

There was no significant difference in AR rates (nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) between newly senescent and old standing stems in either marsh at any sampling time (t-test, p > 0.05). Therefore, data from senescent and old stems are combined in subsequent analyses. Leaves collected from standing dead stems in the natural and transplanted marshes had AR rates similar to stems, both on an areal (cm^2) and ash-free dry weight basis (p > 0.05). The only exception to this occurred in May 1993 when transplanted marsh stems had AR rates (4.26 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) which were significantly higher than AR rates on leaves (1.31 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, t-test, p < 0.01). On an ash-free dry weight basis, however, standing dead stem and leaf AR rates were not significantly different at any sampling time.

The average AR activity on standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems incubated at midday ranged from <1 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} in the natural marsh during November and December to 17 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} on stems collected from the transplanted marsh in July (Table 1; Fig. 1). Midday AR rates were significantly higher than morning or evening AR rates in December and May in the transplanted marsh and in March in the natural marsh. However, in the period July to October, midday AR incubations were equal to or significantly lower than morning or evening incubations (Fig. 1). On most sampling days, AR rates associated with standing dead stems from the natural marsh were equal to or lower than rates associated with stems from the transplanted marsh. The most distinct break in this pattern occurred in April 1991, when AR rates on stems from the natural marsh were significantly higher than those from the transplanted marsh (ANOVA, p < 0.05). This occurred on the first sampling date, after only one growing season, and was the only occasion when well-developed epiphytic films were not observed in the transplanted marsh.

Data from dates on which both natural and transplanted marshes were sampled were used to determine whether marsh type had a significant effect on AR rates (April and October 1991; August, September, November, and December 1992; January, March, and May 1993). The mean AR rates of each marsh type on the selected dates were compared using one-way analysis of variance. This reduced the degrees of freedom but avoided invalid assumptions due to an unbalanced dataset. This conservative approach does not reject the null hypothesis (p = 0.067). As noted above, April 1991 differed from all other sampling dates in that, after only one growing season, no epiphytic films were observed on transplanted marsh stems. Excluding this point from the analysis results in a significant difference in epiphytic AR rates between the natural and transplanted marsh (p = 0.013, 25 d.f.). There also appears to be a temporal pattern in the difference in AR rates between the two marshes. Mean AR rates are most similar from December to June. Mean AR rates are most dissimilar from July to November, when standing dead stems in the transplanted marsh may exhibit AR rates 2–5 times higher than natural marsh stems. DESICCATION EFFECTS In September, exposed stems collected at an early morning low tide, and incubated aerially without prior wetting, exhibited measurable AR rates that were comparable to rates measured on submerged stems collected at the next high tide and incubated aerially (Fig. 2). However, exposed stems collected during the afternoon low tide were visibly more desiccated than the early morning exposed stems, and did not exhibit measurable AR activity. Stems collected at the next high tide had completely recovered AR activity (Fig. 2). Measurable AR activity was detected on exposed, unwetted stems collected from both marshes on four other dates (Fig. 3a,b). In the natural marsh, AR rates associated with exposed, unwetted stems were not significantly different from exposed, wetted stems on any occasion (t-test, p > 0.05). Exposed stems from the transplanted marsh which were wetted prior to incubation always had higher AR rates than unwetted stems, although the differences were significant (p < 0.05) on only two occasions (September 16 and December 9; Fig. 4b). Variability in AR rates was particularly high in these experiments, with the average coefficient of variation equal to 70%. CHARACTERISTICS OF STANDING DEAD MATERIAL The contribution of the epiphytic film to standing dead stem N2 fixation was evaluated in June and December. In June, there was no significant difference in AR rates (nmol C2H4 4-cm section−1 h−1) between intact stems and epiphytic films removed from the stem (ANOVA, p > 0.05) (Fig. 4). However, stems from which the epiphytic film had been removed had significantly lower AR rates (p < 0.05). In December, similar results were obtained, although the differences were only significant for samples from the transplanted marsh (Fig. 4). No significant relationships were observed between ash content and standing dead stem AR rates at any sampling time in either the natural or transplanted marsh (ANOVA, p > 0.05), nor was there a significant relationship when all the data were combined. However, when all leaf data were combined, a small but statistically significant positive relationship between ash content and AR rates (nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) emerged (Fig. 5, p = 0.01, r^2 = 0.2221).

In October 1991, the ash content of the epiphytic film was determined separately from that of the underlying stem. The mean ash content of epiphytic films (36.6% ash) was significantly higher than that of the underlying stems (10.1% ash, t-test, p < 0.05). However, there was no significant relationship between the ash content of epiphytic film and AR rates (nmol C2H4 g AFDW^{-1} h^{-1}, ANOVA, p > 0.05).

The average number of standing dead stems in the natural marsh was 264 stems m^{-2}, while in the transplanted marsh, average standing dead stem density was 135 stems m^{-2} (Table 2).

Discussion

Barring physical perturbation, Spartina alterniflora plants undergo a period of aerial senescence and decomposition after the growing season. In ice-free marshes, standing dead stems may persist for a year or more after senescence, while in more northern latitudes the aerial senescent-decomposition period may be shortened if ice cover pushes stems to the sediment surface. Several previous investigations have demonstrated that standing dead Spartina shoots support greater epiphytic N2 fixation than live shoots (Green and Edmisten 1974; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981). The only critical examination of the relationship between plant senescence and epiphytic N2 fixation was a study by Newell et al. (1992), in which epiphytic N2 fixation rates associated with leaves became detectable 2 wk after senescence, and continued to increase over a 12-wk period. In our study, newly senescent stems, which still retained their upper leaves, did not have significantly different AR rates than older standing dead stems. These observations suggest that not only does epiphytic colonization begin shortly before or just after plant senescence, but that epiphytic N2 fixation rates do not decrease as shoot decomposition progresses.
